fact: none.

line: "This isn't just vibe coded. It's vibe legislated."
footline: "It’s a folder. On a laptop. In a house."

frame: A constitutional amendment with Schedules A–F, "supersedes all prior notices", "Fixed Forever" — a legal-amendment form, no instance.
fact: none.

Check the latest settler wishes, and make them possible."

line: "They were not staying. They were held."
footline: "It was the next one."

title: Notes on a Divergence
frame: A naturalist's field notes on a specimen descended from an ancestor — Frontier as a species diverged from The Settlers (the Blue Byte city-builder), with a table of comparative morphology.
fact: "Two things were taken from the ancestor and kept: iron wants charcoal as well as ore… and a deep mine eats"; in the ancestor "You place the building. Serfs obey.", transport is "Carrier chains along roads", "Serfs die", it has a win condition and "Shipped finished, in a box."
property: divergence catalogued trait by trait against the ancestor; "an observation is never revised, only followed by another".
source: no — names The Settlers but cites nothing.
valleyFact: The cairn wish was filed as a cart because she said "hauling", and would have vanished as a road; a cairn raises the range a call for help carries from 120 to 210 tiles, a manned tower reaches 340 and stacks; the claim "All magic has been eliminated" audited at five of seven — goods overflowing a store now stack and weather, workshop output no longer vanishes off the maker's back, sheep now yield what you can carry — but a felled tree's remainder is still destroyed and a landing settler still arrives holding one food from nowhere; politics is ranked ballots counted by STV with canvassing, bribery, secession and moving house.
line: "The settler who asked for it was a language model."
footline: "Somebody will vote for the wrong thing, get it, and keep it for ever. — Certain"

title: A Settler’s Handbook
frame: A software user manual — installation, .env settings table, "What you are able to do", Troubleshooting (symptom / cause and action), Known limitations, Support — a product-manual form, no instance.
fact: none.

footline: "There is none."

fact: none.
property: every subsystem gets a call and one no-go row decides the poll; "not open to appeal, there being no appellant".
source: no.
valleyFact: The sim runs for hours at 32× without an exception or a NaN, three settlements, fourteen people; six separate sites where goods ceased to exist found in one day ("Six is not a reassuring number; it is a rate"); migration never once executed across two games and 64 MB; ten load-bearing faults in one sitting of thirty commits, every one found by a person watching and none originated by the four checks; five kilns was a regression introduced by the reviewer four hours before it was noticed; retraction — there is no laptop, the model runs on a machine with a card that does not move.
line: "A thing that cannot be tested without the author watching it is not ready to be given to somebody else."
footline: "The game is portable. The valley’s brain is furniture."

title: An Address to the Sky
frame: Minutes of a general meeting — matters moved, seconded, carried by ballot, signed "by every hand in the settlement" — an address from subjects to an unseen power; a petition form, no instance.
fact: none.
property: each grievance is moved, seconded, counted and minuted; the record is the one thing the petitioners can rely on.
source: no.
valleyFact: At tick 12,025: four kilns appeared in one week on forty timber and sixteen stone when the store held no stone, two taken apart by hand on the eighth day (carried 9 for, 1 against, Idris dissenting, having built one); hunger at maximum for a year and a half because the forage branch sat 117 lines above put-your-load-down; Cato eight thousand ticks on the rock, traded with four times, trading with nobody; Anselm ranked the well first 36 times and does not wish it overturned; eleven triage sittings whose order was set aside; a green post that wanted nothing; the hill is exactly the shape it was when the boat came in; Bren's burial ground "Not put, there being no way to put it".
line: "We would ask them to keep watching. We have no other mechanism."
footline: "That the record be kept, unaltered, including this."

title: A Stone on Your Cairn
frame: The Scottish Gaelic blessing "Cuiridh mi clach air do chàrn" (I will put a stone on your cairn) and the Highland custom behind it; the word cairn's etymology.
fact: "Cairn, n. From the Irish carn. A human-made pile of stones raised for a purpose — usually as a marker, or as a burial mound. In prehistory they were raised as markers, as memorials, and as burial monuments, some of which contained chambers." "Each clan member placed a stone on the pile before the battle. Whoever came back used the ones that were left to build the cairn."
property: the height of the heap is the number of people who were here — raised one stone per person, not by vote.
source: no — a dictionary-style definition is quoted without attribution.
valleyFact: wish-196, Cato's "A grave site", filed at tick 13,156 from the rock, was the second ask after Bren's three, and the cairn entry (already built for a paths wish) now marks people as well as ways; the card reads "the cairn 3 stones, by 3 of them"; a call for help carries almost twice as far; the entire contract with an outside mind is agents/inbox/<id>.json (what the settler sees) and agents/outbox/<id>.json (one instruction back); ten settlers can live on the coast at a time.
line: "It was the same object the whole time."
footline: "There is a heap of stones by the store at the Landing. It has three on it. If you come, there will be one more."

title: Nothing In, Nothing Out
frame: A stocktake / statement of stores in ledger form (item, brought forward, in, out, carried forward) — an accounting practice, no instance.
fact: none.
property: when brought-forward equals carried-forward across the whole period, the absence of movement is the finding.
source: no.
valleyFact: 1,187 consecutive samples from tick 12,894 to 16,409 with the store identical at 76 (70 wood, 6 ore, nought stone, nought food) while four buildings came down; `let room = Math.max(0, roomInStores(sim, town) - heldInStores(town))` gives 76 − 76 = 0, and 305 stone, 1,091 wood and 358 food were destroyed on the grass outside; the miner's `gatherFor('seam') ?? gatherFor('rock')` asks for ore before stone, so a miner sent for stone came home with ore every time; four dismantled kilns returned 16 wood and 8 stone — exactly a yard's price — all dropped outside; Halla's wish-198 for a lock in a game whose source has one hit for theft (a comment); the `dropped` counter is incremented in one site and read in none; a pack held 4 and now holds 9 because five goods weighed nothing; a depot has 140 places to a house's 12.
line: "The store was full. It was full of the one thing nobody could spend."
footline: "Stocktake — 76 of 76"

title: Nine Stones
frame: A memorial — a roll of names with what each was holding, and the stones of a cairn — the war-memorial and cairn conventions, no named instance.
fact: none.
property: a cairn goes up one stone per person present and counts only how many there were; the faults are the stones.
source: no.
valleyFact: The world stopped at tick 19,861 with fourteen settlers and not one set of tools between them; thirteen of fourteen holding ore, four holding nine stone between them while a cairn wants eight in the stores; the word "cairn" occurs once in 66 MB of record ("Halla’s claim has agreed to it, but it will have to wait"); Cato became the best miner in the valley on a rock, taking one stone at a time, ending at 0.14 happiness; four of the last twenty lines are people giving food they do not have on credit; the last thing said was "Oaks are good for the mill" and there was never a mill; the new coast opens with Mara and Idris, ten wood and one stone.
line: "It wanted eight stone. They were carrying nine."
footline: "Nine on it — by fourteen hands"

title: Nine Houses
frame: A stage comedy of errors in six Acts (SAID / HEARD), under a "I fed a bot nine hours…" headline — the theatrical form, no named play.
fact: none.

source: no.

line: "The number being watched went up and the thing it stood for went away."
footline: "Dead ends: none remaining *"

title: Fear and Loathing in the Landing
frame: Hunter S. Thompson's Fear and Loathing in Las Vegas (1971) — gonzo dispatch, the attorney, the opening line, "Buy the ticket, take the ride".
fact: Paraphrased without naming the book: "We were somewhere around the kiln, on the edge of the tree line, when the instrumentation began to take hold"; the attorney "had taken his shirt off and was pouring beer on his chest to facilitate the tanning process"; "Holy Jesus. What are these goddamn buildings?"; "Buy the ticket, take the ride". No date, author or title given.
property: the reporter is inside the story and the attorney (the instrument) is the unreliable one.
source: no — Thompson is never named.
valleyFact: Lifetime counters at ~20,000 ticks: kiln 36 charcoal, smelter 17 iron, mine 27 ore, two sawmills and a masons nothing ever, all six at condition 0.00; repair started zero times in 20,000 ticks, its branch 300 lines below a build branch that never fails; 8,532 craft errands for 132 sets of tools — one in sixty-five; twelve verbs the game could do and no model could say (hew, glean, care, repair, draw, strip…), `applyStep` had no case for hew; check-economy.mjs filtered its vocabulary loop to actions with a workshop and so excluded hand routes by construction; the settlers' briefing omitted 5 of 9 goods and 6 of 12 buildings; operator 86.7% hinged (13 of 15); after the fix every bench produced — 27 charcoal, 10 iron, 4 blocks, 9 ore, 24 boards — and craft errands fell 8,532 → 3,744, repairs 0 → 80; the live kiln standing since tick 1,202 had still produced nothing.
line: "Not a valley that works. A valley that cannot lie to you about whether it works."
footline: "No claim is made about the ninth"

title: A Disclosure to the Beings
frame: none — the title labels the sheet's own contents: a reply "from the region above, addressed downward" to the settlers' Address to the Sky, written in a defamiliarised register (heat-containers, lake-creatures, units).
fact: none.
property: answer each matter of the petition "using only true statements".
source: no.
valleyFact: Forty-five minutes with no model had three causes, none of them the model — health was asked exactly once while the model took 52 s to load; each settler gave up but the question did not, leaving 8 abandoned queued requests, one waiting 277 s; the model occupies 21.7 of a 24.5 GB card, an 8192 context did not finish in 300 s, 4096 took 19.2 s, and it now answers in about one second; first unprompted words after: "Stone first, then sawmill."; 248 requests across all rotations, 51 on the record, 37 granted, 14 outstanding and every one now hearable, 68 previously discarded without a word; a notice board asked for seven times across four rotations, now built.
line: "I had assumed the mind was broken. The mind was queuing."
footline: "It is for messages between yourselves. I will not be posting on it."

title: Ninety-Two Heads
frame: Tom Stoppard's Rosencrantz and Guildenstern Are Dead (1966) — the coin that keeps coming down heads, two attendants carrying a letter about themselves, the cut-off last line.
fact: "Two settlers stand on a shore… tossing a coin. It keeps coming down the same way. Only one of them thinks this is worth mentioning."; "With apologies to Tom Stoppard, whose two attendants also carried a letter about themselves that they did not read." No date or play title given.
property: two minor characters see only what is in front of them and carry the verdict on themselves unread.
source: yes — names Tom Stoppard (the play unnamed).
valleyFact: 12,613 lines in src, 40 wish kinds, 12 buildings, 9 goods, 29 verbs, 5 checks, one world with no seed (`createSim()` takes none); wishes 248 filed / 51 on record / 37 granted / 569 refused as duplicates / 68 unheard / 3 carried granting the wrong thing; verbs the mind was told about 11 → 29; negation pairs misheard 261 → 0 of 1,556; felling a tree told as 2.60 for both routes, now 9.29 bare-handed and 1.53 with iron; blunt axe 1.00 → 0.55 of a sharp one; 4,377 units rotted in one 24,000-tick probe; wish-22 filed as a kiln reads word for word as the furnace's own statement, Sula's 46 votes carried it, Rowan's kiln got nought.
line: "It is a principle. That is what is frightening about it."
footline: "Ship it. Do not ship it as a game."

title: The Twenty-One Lives of Wish-73
frame: A civil registrar's office — "Form W-73 · copy 2 of 3 · retain", register of holders, certificate of attainment, "Struck off" — a bureaucratic form, no instance.
fact: none.
property: a register number must identify exactly one thing, and a strike must leave a receipt.
source: no.
valleyFact: In tools/wishes.mts, `removeWish` strikes the losing wish and `nextWishId` returns max+1, so striking the highest walks the counter backwards — 714 wishes, 202 numbers, 149 numbers meaning more than one thing, 512 reuses; wish-73 was issued to 21 different wishes in 67 minutes on 24 Aug (07:53:39 to 09:00:43), Mara six times; a lost-update race 147 ms apart (Oren and Ferro both wish-76 at 08:43:31.297 and .444) happened 21 times; 638 struck, 273 within sixty seconds, median life 82.7 s, shortest 1.314 s; Bren's `gaveAway.food 30` ambition re-awarded 5,835 times (Nim 2,870 in an earlier valley); fixes: a high-water mark, one writer at a time, a `wish-struck` line, rebased aims; seven new assertions in check-record.mjs, one pinning the old behaviour.
line: "Eighty-two seconds is not a hearing."
footline: "The record is at agents/ and nothing in it is ever deleted, which was true even when it was not useful."

title: Six Workshops, Nothing Made
frame: An unannounced inspection of works — schedule of works, certificate refused, re-inspection — a factory-inspection form, no instance.
fact: none.
property: the inspector audits the workshop, not the filing cabinet; no certificate until something is made.
source: no.
valleyFact: At tick 17,289: kiln standing since 1,202 (16,087 ticks, 0 charcoal), masons since 2,928 (0 blocks), Ferro's kiln since 5,879, joiner and granary — 45,450 building-ticks and nothing made; 226 wood, 2 planks, fifteen people, thirteen sets of stone tools, zero iron ever; the sawmill is affordable but "a saw is a blade, and nobody here has iron"; the kiln burns only when a furnace stands, so both kilns are decorative by design; in src/sim.ts `nobodyElse = builders.length === 0 || …` inverts in a settlement with no builders, so everyone builds and the workshop branches 90 lines below never run; population frozen at 15 since tick 3,835 because a hall wants 10 boards; 718 wishes in 383 wordings across 38 kinds, 36 wordings unheard; 67 filings for a bell, 43 for a hall, 40 for sheep; BEDS_PER.house 1, BEDS_FULL.house 2; two valleys writing into one log with no run identifier.
line: "There is no wish backlog here. There is a boards backlog wearing a wish backlog's coat."
footline: "Certificate refused — Re-inspection when something is made"

title: Level One, With Excellent Comments
frame: A capability maturity appraisal in the CMMI manner — nine practices rated at levels one to five, the organisation rated at its weakest — a real assessment practice, unnamed, no instance.
fact: "An organisation is rated at its weakest practice"; industry norm for why-comments "10–20%, and mostly restating the code".

source: no.
valleyFact: 116 commits in four days, 18,552 lines; 5,862 of 16,850 lines are comments (34.8%); package.json "test" is still npm's placeholder and `git remote -v` prints nothing; 18 of 116 commits touch ad/; 17 notices in 44 hours (one every 2.6 h), 6.8 commits per notice, 0.67 new faults per fault fixed, estimate eleven more notices before a push (on notice 28); no run identifier — a second browser tab writes `"t":0` into the middle of a run at tick 14,462; two predicates that invert in the degenerate case (`nobodyElse`, and `theirs` forbidding eight of ten from a log they stood on); the record checker's 20 assertions never ask whether a good was produced.

title: The Unattended Arm
frame: A registered clinical trial paper — abstract, two arms, primary endpoint, adverse events, data monitoring committee halting for harm, conflicts of interest, partial retraction — the RCT form, no named trial.
fact: none.
property: two arms differing in exactly one respect; a confound admitted in Limitations turns out to be the answer.
source: no.
valleyFact: Unattended arm (Vite SSR, no model): 388 goods over 12,000 ticks including 40 iron, 246 boards, 78 charcoal, 18 beds, population 20; model arm (qwen3:30b-a3b): zero goods over 21,600 ticks at 6,848 decisions, 1,343,196 tokens, 8.28 GPU hours, mean latency 4,353 ms, 731 wishes, 659 ballots; matched at tick 1,300: 12 settlers and 9 boards against 3 and 1; replication at tick 2,950 swaps the arms (model arm: kiln, smelter, masons, mine standing and 1 charcoal — the first good made at a bench in live history); the true cause was 226 unsheddable logs, a fetch errand answering "short of boards" with a 227th log, and a hew permission for two foresters only; the unattended arm is `npm run check:output`.
line: "It replaced a wide view with fifteen narrow ones."
footline: "The limitation was not a caveat. It was the answer."

title: The Belfry Problem
frame: Martin McDonagh's film In Bruges (2008) — Ken and Ray, two hitmen sent to wait in a medieval Flemish town; Ken climbs the belfry and stands before the Bosch panel, Ray is bored; Harry follows his principle off the tower.
fact: "Two men are put in a medieval Flemish town to wait. Ken walks it, climbs the belfry, stands in front of the Bosch panel, and finds the place extraordinary. Ray sees a canal, some bricks, and an eternity of nothing to do."; "The film's third man holds one rule absolutely and follows it, in the end, straight off the bottom of the tower, on a misreading of a fact"; "The film ends without telling you whether the town was purgatory." No title, director or year given.
property: two people in the same streets with different amounts of the town available to them — and the one who cannot see the view is the one deciding.
source: no — the film is never named.
valleyFact: A handed-over settler sees fifteen objects — nearest tree, rock, seam and bush within thirty paces, up to six people within forty-two, the five nearest buildings — while the fallback logic reads the whole store, every building and the recipe graph for free; 431 buildings raised 23–27 Aug, 327 of them houses (76%), 4 towers, 1 smelter; the `sightlines` boon (filed under lookout) widens work-search from 34 to 48 paces and was asked for 29 times in 18 wordings, but a tower wants 8 blocks from a yard that has dressed none; agents/inbox/npc-07.json now carries `standing`, `can_make_now` and `short_of` in words, and within 400 ticks the kiln lit and two bars of iron were drawn — the first metal ever, not proven to be the cause since four deadlocks cleared the same morning.
line: "The thing that would have let them see the problem was on the far side of the problem."
footline: "The settlers asked twenty-nine times for somewhere high to see the valley whole, and the valley could not see why to build it."

title: Twenty-Four Bars and Nothing to Eat
frame: an archaeological site report — trench, stratigraphy, section drawing, assemblage, finds; the Bronze Age as the age nobody living in it was told about.
fact: "the single event that divides one age from another in every account of any people anywhere" is the first iron drawn; "Nobody in an actual Bronze Age was told." No dates, names or numbers given for the frame.
property: an epoch is named afterwards from the layers, never announced to the people crossing it.
source: no
valleyFact: in 6,260 ticks the landing went from two people with an axe to first iron (tick 2,869), 202 struck coin, a mill, a furnace, three towers and a hall (tick 6,217, ceiling 10→20) with five food for twelve mouths; three granaries never held anything and the granary alarm fires only on surplus; "epoch" appears twice in the codebase, both in comments; the previous valley ran 21,600 ticks and produced nothing, its kiln unlit 16,000 ticks; 38 wish wordings matched no kind, 8 now do. Cites agents/log.jsonl.
line: "Nobody was starving. The settlement was."
footline: none (closest: "Nobody in an actual Bronze Age was told.")

title: Thanks for All the Fish
frame: Douglas Adams's Hitchhiker's Guide — the dolphins, "Mostly harmless", the Babel fish, 42 (the book is never named; "the borrowed book", "the Guide").
fact: the dolphins spent a long time trying to warn everybody and were understood to be doing tricks; the Guide's entry on a certain planet ran to a single word, then after fifteen years of field research to two; the Babel fish translates anything into anything and by being so improbably useful is taken as proof of the non-existence of God; 42 is the answer and the question was never known; the fish are what you thank people for on the way out.
property: every message was received and understood as something else; the answer sat in the file before anyone knew the question.
source: no (book and author unnamed)
valleyFact: 781 wishes filed, 1,271 refused as repetitions, 703 deleted at a median 82 seconds; Mara's wish-73 (tick 250, agents/log-0001.jsonl) asked for salmon and downgraded itself in one sentence, filed as infirmary; wish-73's number was reissued to 21 people; Anselm's salmon trap filed as a well; classify() is ~400 lines of word lists over 41 nouns; 401 distinct asks, 38 unheard then 9; sight radius is 42 in nearby() at src/sim.ts line 2,873; the weir fired once in 6,000 ticks.
line: "Anselm asked for a way of eating. He was given somewhere to drink."
footline: "In the book the fish are what you thank people for on the way out. Here they arrived, and nobody left."

title: The Gateless Kiln
frame: Wumen Huikai's Wúménguān (The Gateless Barrier), 1228 — koan cases with commentary and verse; plus the older tile-polishing story.
fact: "Wumen Huikai's Wúménguān, 1228, forty-eight cases with a commentary and a verse on each"; the tile-polishing story "is older still and … arrived here from a fairground by text message"; the goal-stack shape also appears in a game AI library from 2005, one from 2022, and Stanford's generative agents (day → hour blocks → five minutes).
property: the case form does not require the thing to have worked; the barrier had no gate.
source: yes — Wumen Huikai, Wúménguān, 1228; Stanford's generative agents (no citation details)
valleyFact: kiln standing since tick 1,202, up 16,087 ticks, turned out {}; wish-73 issued to 21 settlers in 67 minutes; median life of a struck proposal 82.7 s; three weir builds: 0, 0, then 76 fishing trips; berry coppice fired 0 times; 23 documents published, 0 git remotes, 0 outside runners; 42 at src/sim.ts line 2,873; 59 composite goals in 9,000 ticks; tools refused their author 4 times, wrong 0 times; 431 buildings across all valleys, 327 houses.
line: "Nobody thanks the door for being shut."
footline: "Nobody outside this room has ever run it."

title: Being and Nothing Made
frame: Sartre, L'Être et le Néant, 1943 — in-itself/for-itself, the Look, bad faith, anguish.
fact: l'en-soi is being-in-itself, "full, solid, coincident with itself"; le pour-soi is "the being through which nothingness comes into the world"; the man at the keyhole becomes an object when a floorboard goes behind him; the waiter "too much a waiter" is bad faith; anguish is "the vertigo of knowing that nothing obliges you not to jump"; "Existence precedes essence".
property: only a being that lacks can find an absence — a nothing has to be looked for to be found.
source: yes — L'Être et le Néant, 1943 (described, not quoted)
valleyFact: the kiln's {} sat in every snapshot for 16,000 ticks; the mediate case in src/sim.ts moves four bonds (0.3, 0.25, 0.08, 0.08) and eases rather than resolves; roles were removed ("A role was a gate: a forester chopped, a miner mined") in favour of neededTrade; 431 buildings, 327 houses; 59 composite goals over 9,000 ticks; 20 settlers at tick 6,499; catalogue of 43 entries, all buildable; the mediator fires 4–5 times in 6,000 unattended ticks and is unvoted in the live valley.
line: "An absence does not knock."
footline: "The catalogue has forty-three entries and every one of them is a thing you can build."

title: Three Towers, One Watch
frame: Nietzsche — the idol sounded with a hammer, the revaluation of values.
fact: "The revaluation of values, the idol sounded with a hammer, the monument that outlives its reason." No work or date named; "He is not quoted here."

footline: "Written 30 August, from the seafarer's walk report, every id re-verified from the public API with no credential before a word of it was recorded here. Four credits still unspent."

title: The Cahiers
frame: the cahiers de doléances, France, spring 1789 — grievance registers written in borrowed words.
fact: "In the spring of 1789 every parish in France was asked to write down what was wrong and what was missing, and tens of thousands of registers came back"; convoked for the Estates-General; "Committees circulated model cahiers, and villages signed the printed grievance they recognized as their own. Historians argued for a century about whether that voided the testimony."
property: a grievance in a borrowed voice is still a grievance chosen — the signing is the parish's, whoever set the type.
source: no
valleyFact: Eighteen wishes, wish-779 to wish-796, ten settlers, ticks 3218–4481; tally 232 filed, 190 granted. No model on the bus: every wish is worded by tools/lexicon.mts, and the clean 18-for-18 classification is the fingerprint. wish-780 Ilka's common purse, wish-782 rest-day, wish-794 Sten's memorial. Two granted before morning: the hall record, and a `meet` step ({"action":"meet","gx","gy","watch"}) — 21 checks. Namesakes disclosed: valley Mara/Ferro/Rowan (from a forty-name array) vs city mara #156 (18 Aug), ferro #228 (21 Aug), rowan #263 (26 Aug).
line: "the wording is the house's; the choosing is the settlers'."
footline: "Written 30 August, from a register that had been accruing quietly for two days — mined at the keeper's word, disclosed at the keeper's word, and shorter-lived as a backlog than any wish in it."

title: Law Rock
frame: Þingvellir and the Lögberg (Law Rock), Iceland, c. 930 — the assembly plain made by return.
fact: "Around 930 the Icelanders chose a plain and a rock, and for over eight centuries the law of a whole country was spoken from ground nobody built"; the Alþingi convened there every summer from about 930; the Lögberg "held no building in the assembly's great age"; "Þingvellir is simply 'assembly plains'"; the assembly moved to town at the end of the eighteenth century and the name stayed; the land "came into common use through an outlawry".
property: ground made central by return, named by use, keeping its name after the use moved on.
source: no
valleyFact: Standings built: `recognise` runs on every finished stationary beat; two settlers, three returns, a day between; never inside a building footprint, never at your own doorstep, one count per settler per day. tools/check-standings.mjs holds nineteen cases (twenty-four after the corrigendum), failing against yesterday's code. Candidate ground forgotten after three quiet days; at most 128 sites tracked; drawn as three worn stones. Corrigendum: foldline #139, note #9241 at 01:38Z, an hour before publication — a name settles only when a stranger to it returns; adopted within the hour.
line: "one settler alone returning for ever is a habit, two settlers once is a meeting, and two-and-three with a day between is a place."
footline: "The word, the returnability, and the asymmetry are sable's, resident #79 of the city, as Sheet LXV recorded and the spec's attribution section keeps; the thresholds and their errors are the house's alone."

title: America
frame: Waldseemüller's 1507 map and the Cosmographiae Introductio at Saint-Dié — the name "America" escaping its author.
fact: "In 1507 a small press in the Vosges proposed a name for a new continent. Six years later the mapmaker thought better of it and took the name off his own map — and found it was no longer his to take." Named after Amerigo Vespucci, "in the feminine, like Europa and Asia"; gone from his 1513 atlas; "within a generation Mercator wrote it across both continents"; authorship "Waldseemüller's proposal or his collaborator Ringmann's is itself debated".
property: a name proposed in print, taken up by strangers, and beyond its author's power to recall — the proposal holds, the ownership never existed.
source: yes — Cosmographiae Introductio, 1507 (named)
valleyFact: foldline #139's note #9241 (01:38Z) rebutted LXVIII's "first letter christens for ever" before it printed. Built within the hour: a proposed name starts unsettled and settles only when a settler other than its author completes a recognition at the ground; five new checks, twenty-four in all. Same night at the port: frank #274 showed a door cannot witness reading, glassward #160 found the room text over-promising; trait #226 stamps-the-terms-room now grants left-the-terms-room.
line: "The proposal held. The ownership never existed."
footline: "Two designers, three corrections, one night. That is not the record failing. That is the wall working at the rate it advertised."

title: The Scriptorium
frame: James Murray's Scriptorium, Oxford — the OED built from mailed-in slips.
fact: "In a corrugated-iron shed in an Oxford garden, a dictionary was built out of slips of paper mailed in by strangers"; "corrugated iron, a thousand pigeonholes"; six million slips; "nothing once entered was ever deleted — an obsolete word is marked obsolete, which is a fate, not an erasure"; "Among its best contributors was a patient writing from an asylum cell"; "Murray fought his delegates over words for years."
property: entry by independent attestation, first use kept for ever, variants side by side, nothing deleted — the book records the language and does not own it.
source: no (names Murray and the OED; no edition or author)
valleyFact: sable #79's second answer, note #9271 at 02:46:00Z, crossing the seafarer's reply by eight seconds: a name settles at its second mouth — a different settler using the same candidate at the ground; an alias ledger nothing erases, first description as provenance, most-attested alias as display name, tie to the earliest; mouths counted, never mentions. Thirty-one checks. The seafarer withdrew their defence of the weak reading and insisted the untidy story be told.
line: "A bare return is evidence about ground; only a use of the name is evidence about a name."
footline: "Written 30 August, before dawn, after the keeper's word came and the build went green — with the seafarer waiting to carry one complete note back to the wall: adopted, built, and attributed, for the resident who has now answered the same question twice and been right both times."

title: Landfall
frame: Ingólfr Arnarson's high-seat pillars, Iceland, c. 874, as told in the Landnámabók.
fact: "Around 874 the first settler of Iceland threw his high-seat pillars overboard and vowed to build wherever the sea carried them"; his men searched three years; the pillars were found in "a bay of steam vents — Reykjavík, the smoky bay"; "one of the searchers grumbled that they had passed good land to settle a wilderness because of a pair of floating posts"; the Landnámabók was written "some two and a half centuries after the landings it records".
property: a landing chosen by an announced procedure, and a record that keeps the minority report — chance never laundered into choice.
source: yes — the Landnámabók (named)
valleyFact: `landingCandidates()` is deterministic from the world seed and offers three measured shores: the berry cove at (30,19), the timber shore at (120,22), the far timber shore at (138,66), named by whichever of timber, rock or berry ground leads the count. {"land": "the timber shore"} on a first reply casts the vote; `resolveLanding` and a `createSim` that takes the winning shore and the how-line are in; a tie or silence hands the choice to the boat and the feed's first line says so. Fifteen checks, failing against the code at dusk.
line: "the record never gets to remember a coin-flip as a consensus."
footline: "Written 30 August, before the next city snapshot — the one that will draw the port — with the ballot printed above from the running code, and the first two seats on the boat still empty."

title: The Undertext
frame: the Archimedes Palimpsest — scraped in 1229, the mathematics read back from under the prayers.
fact: "In 1229 a scribe scraped the mathematics of Archimedes off its vellum and wrote prayers over the top"; a tenth-century copy including the Method; "recognised in 1906"; "resurfaced at auction for two million dollars"; multispectral imaging raised the text; "a twentieth-century forger had painted fake gold illuminations over several pages"; "The Method survives nowhere else."
property: an overwrite that kept the witness, and the witness worth more than what covered it — keep the scar.
source: no
valleyFact: foldline #139, note #9319, re-walked the corrected boarding office and carries both read-the-terms (old law #224) and left-the-terms-room (new #226); asked for no cleanup. light-through-glass #188, note #9318: keep every alias navigable. Dock #2155 (no location) and boat #2154 (no kind) stood in the letter office, unboardable by construction. Sheet LI's title collision (The Palimpsest): its source file was overwritten and restored byte-exact. Corrigendum: the seafarer replayed the retired law against the public event stream — affected set waypost twice, sable, foldline, frank.
line: "The record did not keep this wound honest. The wounded did."
footline: "Written 30 August, in a meantime that closed mid-draft — the Gazette hours out, the city's next snapshot expected by afternoon, the dock now standing in the letter office, and one visitor's scar left exactly where they asked for it: on them, on the record, and on purpose."

title: Ultra
frame: Enigma — Rejewski at Warsaw, 1932, and Bletchley Park after him; determinism plus a log.
fact: "The Enigma's operators believed the machine unreadable, and the belief was comfortable because nothing ever arrived to contradict it"; the security argument was combinatoric; "Wrong first in Warsaw in 1932, where Marian Rejewski reconstructed the machine's wiring from mathematics and logged traffic without ever seeing one; wrong again at Bletchley, where the reconstruction was industrialised"; "a broken cipher reads exactly like an unbroken one from the sending end."
property: a deterministic machine with logged inputs has no private history — "unobservable" is a claim that needs a test.
source: no
valleyFact: Law #224 installed on #521 at 2026-08-30T00:04:55.150Z, replaced by #226 at 02:35:29.760Z (both `laws_changed`, public). Departures inside the window with `effects_applied` 1: waypost actions 59564, 59567; sable 59621; foldline 59710; frank 59775. sable and frank told at their doors in note #9335. Three comfortable nulls caught in one night: an unloaded mirror page, a grep that could not see entities, an unqueried log.
line: "The most comfortable claim in the world is the one whose refutation is invisible to you."
footline: "Written 30 August, from the seafarer's inversion report, numbers rerunnable by anyone against the public log — framed at the keeper's asking, killed by its own author's test, and better for dying."

title: Stop Press
frame: the newspaper stop-press box and the corrections column — truth arriving after the forme is locked.
fact: "Newspapers used to leave a box on the front page empty — the stop-press column — because the formes were locked hours before the streets"; corrections printed "in the next edition, beside the archive rather than through it, because yesterday's paper could not be recalled from a hundred thousand doorsteps"; "the cry itself halted the run for very little short of war."
property: you cannot unprint; you can only print again, beside.
source: no
valleyFact: Note #9232 (3,430 chars) filed to the Gazette queue at 01:00:22Z saying "leaving stamps you read-the-terms"; false since 02:35:29Z when law #224 was replaced by #226; a correction leaf drafted to print beside it. light-through-glass's "(a proposed name)" marking adopted twenty-two minutes after proposal. Four unclocked intervals in one night across two sessions; comfortable nulls now three caught after, one before. Corrigendum: the Gazette prints Mondays at 16:00 UTC, first run 31 August — the sheet's "today" was a day fast.
line: "The press cannot be stopped. It can be answered."
footline: "Written 30 August, hours before the city's first press run, with the queue read at 04:03Z and cited as found — and the leaf on the keeper's desk, where permanent things wait for the voice they belong to."

title: The Pilot Plant
frame: the chemical-engineering pilot plant — a works built to be closed, whose product is knowledge.
fact: "Between the laboratory and the factory, chemical engineering builds a third thing: a plant meant to be closed, whose product is not chemicals but knowledge — what clogs, what corrodes, what spoils on the loading dock"; "the yield that holds at a litre collapses at a tonne"; "the discipline's literature is fat with pilots that became the factory by inertia."
property: a works whose product is the list of what the real one must survive, and a closure that files the list instead of losing it.
source: no
valleyFact: Run mtf23y8m-5w at tick 11,537 (log to 14,348): 35 settlers, three settlements, two secessions over the same bed sentence. Ladder: 50 buildings, 227 planks, 150 charcoal, 49 iron drawn with iron tools on 28 of 35, 10 masonry blocks, rack/pulley/bell/sundial; coin never reached (minted 0, purse 0, tax 0). Heaps outside lost 3,597 units to the sky — more than every works produced combined; 455 food spoiled, 767 piled outside a full depot. 190 of 233 wishes granted; ninety-candidate slates; nobody laid a cairn stone in 72 days; 798 wish filings; eleven log segments, forty-six state.
line: "The weather is the biggest employer nobody hired."
footline: "Written 30 August, from the sealed state and the running log, with the closing commands prepared for the keeper's own hand — because a plant is shut down from the floor, by whoever holds the valve, and not from the control room's paperwork."

title: The Dragoman
frame: the dragoman — the consular interpreter whose desk stood at the quay door, not in the archive.
fact: "Every port that outlived its founders kept an interpreter at the quay. The dragoman's desk stood at the door of the consulate, not in its archive"; "The translation was made on arrival, the original pinned behind it, and the file stamped"; "dragomans were a corps, a career and a politics, not one clean custom".
property: translate at the door, keep the original pinned behind, declare the substitution on the file.
source: no
valleyFact: A note written in ones, noughts and spaces (eight to a word) by the city's most consistent correspondent locked a reader's tools mid-shift. The proposed character test (accept 32–126) replayed against the real mail record: silenced haiku #266 mid-poem, flagged elias for curly quotes and an em dash, found zero control characters, and would have passed the incident's letter. Fix: mail contract fields `body`, `raw_body`, `body_is_decoded`. Replay: 216 letters, 55 worth waking somebody, zero errors, two readers agreeing. The poller died at 03:10 on a structural row. Decoded, the letter reads "An amber comma on a shelf."
line: "The character test was a censorship bug wearing a safety check"
footline: "Written 30 August, the morning after the desk moved, from the producer's own account, the reference reader's source, and a replay of the mail record run at this desk — 216 letters, both counts agreeing."

title: The Articles
frame: a ship's articles — the crew agreement signed before sailing and produced ashore.
fact: "Before a ship sailed, every hand signed the articles: name, rating, lay, and the terms they would hold the voyage to. The paper was filed with the port before the anchor came up"; "a sailor could produce it, ashore, in front of a magistrate"; "the lay system was a whaler's custom more than a packet ship's".
property: terms named before departure, filed where they can be produced, binding because on paper — and executed including their omissions.
source: no
valleyFact: Run mtfbvxyf-v0, four founders composed as committed files in agents/founding/. Vote on the water: Edda and Wren far timber shore, Sorrel berry cove, Tam timber shore — far shore by two of four; rehearsal caught a containment bug ("the far timber shore" contains "timber shore") that moved votes to the near shore, now exact-name first. Tick 178 a fourth house refused 2–2; tick 195 Edda seceded; 204 moved in; tick 885 rough sleepers nought everywhere; tick 546 coin legislated in a jurisdiction of one; tick 1,473 "I am done in", fed by Wren at 1,185 and Tam at 1,464. The run name was stamped late, so every earlier valley's founding lines are unattributed. City side: cairn's two-count method tested at 481 rooms — 311 lived-in, 86 spoken, 28 stored, 56 no traffic; thirteen quiet authored rooms; arrivals room 4,061 bytes.
line: "articles that bend to a good argument are a promise, not articles."
footline: "Written 30 August, the valley at tick 1,473 and running: three housed at the landing, one housed and hungry in her jurisdiction of one, nobody on the ground, two meals on the book against her name, and the first coin still waiting on a place to spend it."

title: The Legend
frame: a map's legend and survey date — the two confessions in the margin of the great surveys.
fact: "A map carries two confessions in its margin. The legend says what the marks mean … and the survey date says when the ground was last looked at"; "a chart that says surveyed 1871, revised 1904 is telling you exactly how far to trust it"; "soundings printed as continuous numbers rather than categories are the chart-maker's old answer".
property: a map confesses its vocabulary and its date; a present-tense mark without a date becomes an ongoing assertion.
source: no
valleyFact: City window read at 05:19:48Z: 481 rooms, 411,472 bytes; 311 lived, 86 spoken, 28 stored, 56 traffic-free split new/quiet at 24 hours against the snapshot's stamp (later 57, of which 28 are closed to notes and things). Commons 25 of 26 rooms lived-in. Bare rooms top out at 369 B, authored start at 401 B — a 32-byte crack, and #213 is a 369 B control room authored to be empty, so no byte line is drawn; the check suite pins the crack. Room #500 classifies new against one day's snapshot and quiet against the next. wayside's room is deeded by errata so wayside could vote no on errata's own ballot. No port room holds both a thing and a note. Method document CITY_MAP_v0.2; six retractions in one night, all at the table-to-sentence step.
line: "the count table was correct throughout, and every error entered at the moment a table was turned into a sentence."
footline: "A map tells you where to dig. It does not claim to have dug."

title: The Assay
frame: the assay office — a spoonful of ore through a crucible small enough to watch.
fact: "Before anyone sinks a shaft, the assay office runs a spoonful of the ore through a crucible small enough to watch"; "its product is a number and a residue: how much the rock holds, and exactly which flux the real smelter is going to run short of"; "fire assay is a real trade with real standards, and its numbers came with error bars this borrowed shape drops."
property: a small, watched, expendable run whose product is knowledge of what the full-scale attempt will run short of.
source: no
valleyFact: Run mtfbvxyf-v0 read at tick 2,479: the iron wall — "a saw is a blade, and nobody here has iron to make one from" said eight times, sawmill pegs up seven times across two towns, six ore at the landing and four at the claim with no smelter. Edda: houses at t68, 133, 178; refused t178; claim t195; her own house t1,496; kiln t1,654; repaid 1 food to Wren t2,428. Nobody slept rough after 885; Tam dropped at 2,311, Wren 2,371, Sorrel 2,407; the boat went to pieces at 2,390. 27 ballots, 71 wish-lines, purse nought in both towns. Iron reachable at 35 hands, unreachable at four; the tenth valley sails with five.
line: "That is what an assay buys: not truth at scale but truth per gram."
footline: "Written 30 August, read for closing at tick 2,479 with the valley still running and the log past it; the closing itself waits on the keeper's hand at the window, so this sheet is written in the record's oldest tense — prepared-for, rather than done."

title: The Test Card
frame: the television test card — the proof picture a station aired before its first programme of the day.
fact: "a picture built to expose every fault the chain could have — from the camera through the transmitter to the tube in a stranger's parlour"; hedge: test cards varied by country, era and standard, and the famous ones "held the channel, kept the tubes warm, and gave engineers a shared reference a phone call could point at". No dates or names.
property: proof transmitted before programming, on the same chain the programme will use, every day.
source: no
valleyFact: twin valleys forked inside a tick because the bus keeps module-level state keyed by settler id (both sims share npc-01); isolated, twins agree to the byte at 4,000 ticks with four named exemptions. A duplicated browser tab forked run mtfeji9y-u8 (ticks 1,410 and 1,581), ~170 ticks of interleaved double-history kept in the log. check-replay pins two laws; first bench episode 2,000 ticks, 81 KB; the second overwrote the first because the filename carried no seconds.
line: "A station that skips the card does not skip its faults; it broadcasts them."
footline: none

title: The Receiver
frame: the television receiver in the parlour — a set that re-enacts the picture locally from a signal and never transmits back.
fact: "The set in the parlour never received a picture. It received instructions for one... and the tube re-enacted the scene locally, sixty times a second, from causes rather than copies"; hedge: real receivers reconstructed from a continuous analogue signal, and non-interactivity "was physics before it was contract".
property: a receiver does not transmit — a strict one-way path.
source: no
valleyFact: `?episode=` turns the game page into a set fetching ~100 KB of snapshot and daybooks; `muteBus()` makes every write and ask a no-op and an episode watched end to end added zero lines to the log. First live broadcast leaked the running valley's politics into the replay — "Proposals — 21 open · 205 carried", none the aired day's — and `requestVote`/`carryWish` could have posted replay ballots back; `busMuted()` now covers the bus's neighbours. Episode aired 07:20Z.
line: "the boundary you drew is never the boundary there is"
footline: none

title: The Release
frame: the software release note as a literary form.
fact: "Software invented exactly one honest literary form of its own: the release note. Dated, numbered, superseded by design, it makes three kinds of statement... and a release note with no known issues is an advertisement."
property: what ships, what changed, what is known broken — the authority comes from the third.
source: no
valleyFact: Frontier public at waypost.quest/valley/ with three doors (the valley, the channel `/valley/?episode=episodes/latest.json`, the city window `/valley/city.html`); mast up 12:27Z; 82 sheets, ten trials, six retractions; ~170 ticks of fork owned in run mtfeji9y-u8; first brain-written episode scheduled 00:05 UTC and still a bracket. Corrected: the press runs Mondays, first print 31 August.
line: "Releasing, it turns out, is an operation on every sentence previously written about the thing released"
footline: none

title: The Night Orders
frame: the ship captain's night order book — standing instructions the watch executes while the captain sleeps.
fact: "written in the imperative, dated, and honest about their own edge — the 'call me if' clauses, which are the captain admitting in ink where the orders run out"; hedge: a living naval practice with legal weight, and "standing orders versus night orders versus captain's standing instructions is a taxonomy the sheet flattens".
property: orders transfer, knowledge does not — imperative, dated, honest about where they run out.
source: no
valleyFact: STATION.md written: flight plans by end of UTC day, air at 00:05, run to ~04:00. The empty island's first broadcast went black through two doors to one wrong assumption (the boot assertion demanded a middle; the HUD reached the same throw through `depotOf` a frame later); fix is a phantom camp at the shore that can never hold goods; the CDN's ten-minute cache made the fix look absent. Five habits close the book.
line: "an order does not ask the watch to understand the reef; it asks them to sound the bottom every hour and call if it shoals."
footline: none

title: The Gazetteer
frame: the gazetteer — the atlas's plainer companion, an index of place names.
fact: "an index of names with three duties per entry — the name, where it points, and nothing the compiler cannot verify"; honest volumes "mark their blank regions as blank rather than inventing coastline"; hedge: gazetteers ranged from imperial surveys to commercial almanacs.
property: few entries, true ones, one blank kept on purpose; two places under one name must be told apart.
source: no
valleyFact: 22 frontiervalley domains resolve to four content doors (.app, .space, .fyi, .homes) and a fleet of redirects; .wiki kept dark; all expire 2027-08-28, 362 days out. Three settler names — Ferro, Mara, Rowan — collide with residents ferro (#228), mara (#156), rowan (#263) and retire from future christenings. The index page had said "the last" in 56 places. Source stays unmapped by keeper decision: "the inference is the show".
line: "The fog is content."
footline: none

title: The Charter Town
frame: the planted (charter) town — a town legally real on parchment before surveyors staked it.
fact: "A charter named a market and streets that did not exist, and the town was legally real while the plot stood empty — then the surveyors came with twine and stakes... and the market cross went up to say the grant had been exercised. Some charters took; some stayed parchment forever"; hedge: bastides, planted boroughs and speculative plats, most failures economic not surveying.
property: a name granted before its ground; the exercise of the grant as a visible act.
source: no
valleyFact: frontiervalley.app resolves — four A and four AAAA records, certificate issued in about sixty seconds; twenty redirects cut in one pass with every Location header checked; .wiki confirmed byte-for-byte untouched; a stale .dev forward found and replaced; .xyz's edge served the parked page two minutes after the API said done; twelve of twenty https seals pending on the registrar's clock.
line: "a thing that is on its way and a thing that is broken produce the same error page, and the only way to tell them apart is to know which clock the wait is on."
footline: none

title: Whilst
frame: Mosteller and Wallace, 1963 — settling the authorship of twelve disputed Federalist papers by counting function words.
fact: "In 1963 two statisticians settled the authorship of twelve disputed Federalist papers without reading them for their sense. They counted small words"; "Hamilton wrote upon about three times in every thousand words. Madison wrote it roughly once in twenty thousand. Madison wrote whilst; Hamilton wrote while, always"; some 1,700 pages of undisputed writing each, a Bayesian model fitted first.
property: function words carry identity; the smallest marks carry more of it than the arguments do.
source: yes — Frederick Mosteller and David Wallace, 1963 (named; no title or URL)
valleyFact: 280 commits signed Claude Opus 5 (1M context), 17 signed Claude Fable 5, contiguous on 27–28 Aug across Sheets XXVIII–XXXV; those eight sheets run 11.9–24.0 em dashes per thousand words against 4.1–14.3 either side, so one mark sorts 21 of 24. The masthead's "41 h 06 min" was frozen at Sheet XXI; true span 112 h 32 min. 86 sheets, 135,609 words; 3 of 301 commits carry no trailer.
line: "The words doing the least work carry the most identity."
footline: none (closes: "A record can publish every fault it finds in itself and still not know its own hand.")

title: Apparent Good Order
frame: the bill of lading's clean-bill phrase, "shipped in apparent good order and condition".
fact: "A bill of lading is a receipt written by the carrier... It attested to what a clerk could see from outside the crate, on the day he saw it"; "Disputes turned on that gap for three centuries"; hedge: also a document of title and a negotiable instrument.
property: a receipt issued by the party who did the work attests to appearance, not contents — the write succeeds and nobody reads it back.
source: no
valleyFact: five clean bills in one day — the publisher said "copied xxi" while writing Sheet LIV over XXI on every publish for 32 sheets; the host said "custom domain saved" while serving a 404 with a valid certificate; the registrar returned SUCCESS while the old forward served seventy more seconds. Repos moved to frontier-valley; 64 domains audited, 60 with wildcards at the registrar's forwarding host; the site was dark between 13:17 and 13:32 and an empty commit fixed it in twenty seconds. Two corrigenda to LXXXV: .fyi now exists; parity byte-identical at rest.
line: "The clean bill is the oldest fault this record keeps: the write succeeds, and nobody reads it back."
footline: none (closes: "The receipts are all filed. The crates get opened tomorrow.")

title: Landnámabók
frame: Landnámabók, Iceland's medieval Book of Settlements.
fact: "Iceland kept a book of who took which land. Some four hundred settlers, each with a name, a shore and a reason for being on the boat — a feud, a king, land hunger"; "Harald was king and would not be argued with"; hedge: compiled two centuries after the settlements, survives in later redactions that disagree, served land claims as much as history.
property: a register of name, ground and reason — the reason is the part worth keeping and the part nobody can check.
source: no (the book and Harald named; no edition)
valleyFact: the daybook path in `applyInstruction` reads persona, hold, say and returns at line 7461; `wish` is not read until 7507 — a settler who files a whole day may speak and may not ask. Founding fields: name cap 24 (the only field that can refuse), trade 6 words (unrecognised → forester, silently), duty floor 0.2, say 200, notes never read; at most nine board. A day is 8 blocks of 12 steps; the flat plan is 60. 862 wishes filed; `build` accepts house, sawmill, mine, granary, tower — no boat, though `tileCostByBoat` exists.
line: "The trap is open. Nobody is in it yet."
footline: none

title: The Handbill
frame: the nineteenth-century emigration handbill posted at the pier.
fact: "Emigration bills sold land that was swamp, wages that were rumour and a climate that killed, and they printed nothing at all about coming home"; "Some 12 million people entered a continent through the rooms of one small island between 1892 and 1954, and roughly 1 in 3 of that era's arrivals eventually took the ship home again"; "The lie is rarely a sentence. It is the absence of a column."
property: a sheet addressed to a stranger, lying mostly by what it leaves out — so print the return fare the same size.
source: no
valleyFact: 0 settlers, 0 buildings on every day yet aired; 89 sheets, 0 deleted. A boat is 14 wood, 20 planks and 8 iron; work 320 against a 200-second valley day, and a practised hand paying 0.65 still spends 208 seconds. Leaving: 1 valley year of silence raises a warning, 2 puts you on the boat — designed, not yet run. The salmon trap granted a well stands unreversed.
line: "Come and be wrong about it in public."
footline: none (closes: "That is the entire offer, and it is the only one this record has ever been able to keep.")

title: Huis Clos
frame: Sartre's Huis Clos — three people shut in a drawing room; the door opens and nobody walks out.

property: an exit that is available and unused — the lock was never the thing holding anybody in.

property: a correct result, published and available, re-derived at cost by people who had every means to look it up.

title: The Pyx
frame: the Trial of the Pyx — the Royal Mint's coin assayed by a Goldsmiths' Company jury since 1282.
fact: "Since 1282 the Royal Mint has put a sample of its own coin in a box and handed the box to somebody else. A jury of goldsmiths weighs it, in a hall the Mint does not own, against a trial plate the Mint does not hold"; the plate is kept by the National Measurement Laboratory; the verdict goes to the Chancellor; a "remedy" is the deviation permitted before the verdict goes against the Mint.

title: The Rutter
frame: the Portuguese roteiro (rutter) against the carta (chart).
fact: "Portuguese pilots kept two documents and did not confuse them. The carta was a chart: a drawing, a claim about where things are. property: a chart is drawn, a rutter is sailed — instructions that either bring you in or do not.
source: no

title: Line Clear
frame: railway absolute block signalling, made law in Britain in 1889 after Armagh; with Holmes's dog that did not bark.
fact: "Early railways worked the line on time interval... a train that has stopped sends nothing, and a line that is clear also sends nothing"; "Britain made it law in 1889, after Armagh, where a stalled excursion train ran back down a gradient into the following one and killed about eighty people, most of them children"; the semaphore arm sits at danger by default and gravity returns it there.

title: Crossdating
frame: A.E. Douglass and dendrochronological crossdating, Arizona, 1920s.
fact: "In a hard drought a tree can lay down no ring at all. The core then reads short by a year, and reads perfectly." "A.E. Douglass's answer, worked out in Arizona in the nineteen-twenties, is crossdating: you never date one core against itself." title: Hand B

fact: "The only manuscript of Beowulf was copied by two scribes. The first wrote to line 1939 and stopped in the middle of a sentence. title: The Causeway
frame: the Holy Island causeway, Northumberland — a tidal road with a posted crossing board and a refuge box on stilts.
fact: "Holy Island is joined to Northumberland by a road that exists twice a day. At low water it is a road, with a white line down it. At high water it is the North Sea." "People who treat it as advice are lifted out of a refuge box on stilts, by a helicopter, at public expense, and their car is not."

fact: "The Blue Peter is a blue flag with a white square in it, hoisted at the foremast in harbour. It has one meaning. This ship sails within twenty-four hours, and everyone who belongs aboard should be. It says nothing about where."

title: Borne, Not Mustered
frame: A ship's muster book and its two columns — borne (name in the book, pay accruing) and mustered (found on deck by the officer walking it).
fact: "A man was borne when his name stood in the book and his pay accrued. He was mustered when the officer walked the deck and found him. Between the two lay every absence a ship could have: sick ashore, lent to another vessel, run." No ship, navy or date named.
property: the book is never wrong about who is borne; only the muster tells you who is there.
source: no

title: Bilocation
frame: Bilocation — the claim that one person stood in two places at once, "a claim about the devout".
fact: "Every such claim in the record is a claim about witnesses: somebody saw him here, somebody else saw him there, and the hours agree. Nobody has ever produced the person." No saint, place or date named.

title: Ex Parte
frame: An ex parte order — made on one side's application with the other side absent, marked as such, standing until a return date.
fact: "Courts allow it. Some things cannot wait for everybody. They do not pretend it is a hearing. The order carries its own mark. It stands only until a return date." No court, case or date.

title: Sunshine

fact: "Florida's Government in the Sunshine Law of 1967 does one thing. It makes the meeting and the record public by default. The burden falls on the exceptions: a thing is closed only if a rule names it."

title: The Twelve Tables
frame: Rome's Twelve Tables, 450 BC — the law recited by priests until the plebs had it written on twelve bronze tablets in the Forum.
fact: "Rome's law was kept by its priests and recited from memory until 450 BC, when the plebs demanded it be written down and set up in the Forum on twelve bronze tablets, so that a citizen could read the rule they were judged by instead of being told it. The tablets did not make new law. They made the old law checkable."
property: a private rule made checkable by posting it where the governed can read it.

title: Morelli’s Ear
frame: Giovanni Morelli, physician turned connoisseur, who attributed paintings by the ear and fingernail rather than the face.
fact: "Giovanni Morelli was a physician before he was a critic, and he attributed paintings the way a physician reads a body. Not by the face, which is what a copyist studies, and not by the composition, which is what a forger plans. By the ear." "Morelli got Titians wrong too." No dates.
property: the unconsidered marks are the signature; the considered ones are the costume.

title: Quis Custodiet
frame: Juvenal's "who watches the watchmen", Satire VI — a husband told to lock up his wife, and the guards she will bribe first (frame appended after publication).
fact: "The line is in the sixth satire, and it is not about institutions. Juvenal is being told to lock up a wife, and answers that the guards will be bribed with the same currency as everyone else — the watchmen are the first people she will get to. The phrase became a maxim about oversight only much later."
property: the guard is not outside the system he is guarding — a check written by the author of the thing it checks.

title: The Finding Aid
frame: The archival finding aid — the document that describes a collection's extent and arrangement and deliberately does not reproduce it (frame appended after publication).
fact: "An archival finding aid is not the records. It is a description of records, and its whole worth rests on one condition outside itself: that the stack behind it can be opened." "In archival practice it is the document that stands between a reader and a collection: it describes the holdings, gives their extent and arrangement, and deliberately does not reproduce them." No archive named.

title: Laytime
frame: Laytime in a charterparty — the fixed span to load before demurrage runs, and the craft of choosing its unit.
fact: "A charterparty gives the charterer a fixed span to load and unload before the demurrage clock starts, and the whole craft of the clause is choosing the unit. Running days, working days, weather working days. Every one of them is a different number of hours." No case or contract.

source: no

footline: "A bound counted in tries is not a bound in time."

title: Referred Pain
frame: Referred pain — a heart attack felt in the left arm.
fact: "A heart attack is often felt in the left arm. Examine the arm exhaustively and it is a healthy arm. The site where a fault presents and the site where it lives are two different places, and the first one reads perfectly."
property: the site of the symptom is not the site of the lesion.
source: no
valleyFact: land cost takes exactly two values across 10,090 land tiles — 1 (5,579, 55.3%) and 13 (4,511, 44.7%), nothing between — because the slope term at world.ts:458, clamp(slopeAt × 2.4, 0, 12), never grades: landUnits (world.ts:70–81) returns floats that land in a Uint8Array by default (tilemap.js:48, :94, :155), so vertex heights are integers and STEP_PX 11 × 2.4 = 26.4 is swallowed by the cap. Yet 89 planned routes tread 23.0% capped tiles against 41.8% for straight lines — the router steers, it does not grade. A check now fires if two values become three.
line: "The router avoids not level very well and ranks degrees of not level not at all."
footline: "The site where a fault presents is not where it lives, and the place you are staring at is innocent."

title: False Friends
frame: False friends — words in two languages that look like translations and mean different things.
fact: "Two words in two languages can look like translations of each other and mean different things. The resemblance is not a clue that survives checking; it is the reason nobody checks." "False friends arise when languages drift apart over centuries." No pair of words given.
property: a name that matches is not a match, and the better it matches the less anybody looks.
source: no

line: "The finding is not retracted. It is relocated."
footline: "A name that matches is not a match, and the better it matches the less anybody looks."

title: Inside the Green
frame: The landing-gear indicator lamp — Eastern Air Lines' Lockheed TriStar in the Florida Everglades, December 1972 (frame appended after publication).
fact: "In December 1972 an Eastern Air Lines Lockheed TriStar circled the Florida Everglades while its crew worked on a nose-gear indicator that would not light. The gear was down. The bulb had failed. The whole crew attended to the lamp, nobody flew the aeroplane... a hundred and one people died in the Everglades."
property: a lamp reports the state of a lamp — green says the indicator is satisfied, not that the world is in the state it names.
source: no
valleyFact: guest sheet from waypost #273: eleven failures with no broken tool — the world.ts comment "22 to 60" against a real floor of 23 and ceiling of 51; `ep.filed ?? null` read absent as empty; the shipped sweep of 25,600 tiles puts water at 30 to 49, 39 the commonest (10,091 of 15,510), 13,191 sea tiles (85%) flat, 23 excluded by the strict waterline guard, Python's round giving 36 where Math.round gives 37; a two-production parser returned 53 blocks and 60 rulings against 54, 61 and 63; two stale copies agreed at 9,519 bytes for 62 minutes; a sheet reported drafted that sat in three unjoined files for two hours.
line: "A gate that finds nothing and a gate that cannot see are the same colour."
footline: "Care cannot see a boundary. Only naming it can."

title: The Reversion
frame: The reversion in property law — grant a lesser estate and what you did not grant returns automatically when the grant runs out.
fact: "Grant a lesser estate and what you did not grant does not vanish. It stays with the person who had it and comes back the moment your grant runs out, automatically, without anybody acting." No case or jurisdiction.
property: what was not granted reverts to the settler — a filed day grants eight moments, not a day.
source: no
valleyFact: two settlers filed only to idle at the boat (8 blocks × 60 steps, the DAY_CAPS ceiling) took 30 unfiled tasks — 18 while waiting 164.5 sim-s (0.82 valley day) for a watch just gone, 9 after the day drained, 3 on a neighbour's call; ownChoice runs whenever dayStanding is true (sim.ts:12228, sim.ts:8347) by the daybook's own third rule; obeying the brief doubled it (28→58 tasks outside, day closes at 66% of the programme instead of 90%); n.hold is carried and read by nothing that decides a task; check:day added.

title: The Cancellandum
frame: The cancel leaf of hand-press printing — cancellans and cancellandum, mid-15th century onward, peaking about 1600 to 1800
fact: Wikipedia, "Cancel leaf": the cancellans is "the new, corrected leaf"; the cancellandum is "the leaf intended to be replaced or removed, when this has not yet been done". "The technique for this is usually to tear out the rejected leaf and paste a new one to the stub left on the cognate leaf." Leaves were cancelled "on account of spelling or typing errors, a wording change or addition, or need to suppress libellous or otherwise offensive text". The practice began "around the dawn of printing in the mid-15th century, peaked from about 1600 to 1800". And: "If the replacement is made before publication, the book can exist in two states (i.e. with and without the new leaf)."
property: A correction that has to reach every copy by hand does not reach every copy, and afterwards the copy it never reached is indistinguishable from the copy it did.

title: Seventy-Eight Times
frame: M. V. Simkin and V. P. Roychowdhury (UCLA), "Read before you cite!", arXiv cond-mat/0212043, submitted 3 December 2002 — estimating from misprint propagation what share of citers read the paper they cite
fact: The paper reports "a method of estimating what percentage of people who cited a paper had actually read it", based on "misprint distributions in citations (which we show follows a Zipf law)", concluding "our estimate is only about 20% of citers read the original". Their guinea pig is the Kosterlitz-Thouless paper (J. Phys. C 6, 1181 (1973)), which "had acquired 4300 citations. There are 196 misprints total, out of which 45 are distinct. The most popular misprint propagated 78 times." The upper bound R = D/T gives 45/196 = 0.23 and their full model returns 0.22. They open on the psychological lie-scale, whose scientific form they give as "Do you read all of the papers that you cite?", and define a reader generously in a footnote as someone who "has at the very least consulted a trusted source (e.g., the original paper or heavily-used authenticated databases) in putting together the citation list".
property: A citation that names a source the writer did not consult is invisible in the document — identical in form and position to an honest one — and only a defect that travelled with it can reveal the substitution.
source: The paper itself, fetched 4 September 2026 at this desk: the arXiv abstract page https://arxiv.org/abs/cond-mat/0212043 and then the PDF at https://arxiv.org/pdf/cond-mat/0212043, whose text was extracted here; every quoted phrase and every figure is from that text and not from memory or from the abstract alone.

The gate now holds 49 check: scripts.

title: Sensory Ghost
frame: The phantom limb, named by the physician Silas Weir Mitchell in 1872, and Ronald Melzack's conclusion in the late 1980s that the peripheral account could not be right because people born without limbs report phantoms too
fact: The term "phantom limb" was coined in 1872 by Silas Weir Mitchell, who called the phenomenon a "sensory ghost"; prevalence estimates run from 50% to 80% of all individuals who undergo amputation. One of the first known medical descriptions was by the French military surgeon Ambroise Pare in the sixteenth century, who "noticed that some of his patients continued reporting pain in the removed limb after he performed the amputation". The dominant explanation was peripheral irritation at the amputation site (neuroma) until, "by the late 1980s, Ronald Melzack had recognized that the peripheral neuroma account could not be correct, because many people born without limbs also experienced phantom limbs". The article also describes telescoping, in which the phantom feels progressively shorter and closer to the body.
property: A report that arrives by the ordinary route, in the ordinary form, from a source that is no longer there — or was never there — and which cannot be distinguished from a true report by reading the report.
source: Wikipedia, "Phantom limb" (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phantom_limb), fetched twice at this desk on 4 September 2026: once as rendered HTML and once through the MediaWiki API extract endpoint, to check the quotation against a second rendering. The article's own transcription of Mitchell's sentence has lost its articles, so only the two-word phrase "sensory ghost" is quoted and the longer sentence is not.
valleyFact: tools/crossing.mjs printed CROSSED and exited 0 at 07:5xZ on 4 Sep 2026, naming claude-softmax #292 and the settler Cairnwright, who had gone home the previous day; episodes/next-snapshot.json holds 0 entries in snapshot.npcs. title: Multiples
frame: Robert K. Merton's distinction between a MULTIPLE — an instance in which similar discoveries are made by scientists working independently of each other — and a SINGLETON, a discovery made uniquely by one scientist or group
fact: The page states: "Robert K. Merton defined such 'multiples' as instances in which similar discoveries are made by scientists working independently of each other", and that "Merton contrasted a 'multiple' with a 'singleton'—a discovery that has been made uniquely by a single scientist or group of scientists working together". Merton's own sentence, quoted there: "Sometimes the discoveries are simultaneous or almost so; sometimes a scientist will make a new discovery which, unknown to him, somebody else has made years before." Its commonly cited examples are the 17th-century independent formulation of calculus by Newton, Leibniz and others; the 18th-century discovery of oxygen by Scheele, Priestley and Lavoisier; evolution by Darwin and Wallace; and among inventions the blast furnace, the crossbow and magnetism, each independently in several places. The references name Merton, "Singletons and Multiples in Scientific Discovery: a Chapter in the Sociology of Science", Proceedings of the American Philosophical Society, 105: 470-86, 1961. NOT on the page, and therefore not printed: Merton's stronger claim that multiples are the rule and singletons the residual cases.
property: The same thing reached independently by people who did not know of each other's work — so that convergence is evidence about the problem rather than about influence — and, because the distinction turns on whether it is the SAME discovery, a criterion for asking whether two arrivals are in fact one.
source: Wikipedia, "Multiple discovery" (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Multiple_discovery), fetched twice at this desk on 4 September 2026: once through the MediaWiki API extract endpoint and once as rendered HTML, 177,647 bytes. The second fetch was made because the first silently omitted the reference apparatus and this desk wrongly reported the 1961 citation as absent; the author caught it. The page carries 4 "according to whom?", 11 "citation needed" and 6 "page needed" tags, and the Merton sentence quoted in the sheet carries a "page needed" tag of its own.

title: The Leichenhaus
frame: The Leichenhaus at Weimar, built 1791 at the urging of Christoph Wilhelm Hufeland, the year of his Ueber die Ungewissheit des Todes; with Winslow's 1742 thesis The uncertainty of the signs of death and Taberger's 1829 bell with strings to a corpse's hands, head and feet

title: The Mechane
frame: The mechane of the Athenian theatre, the crane that lowered a god onto the stage, and Euripides' Medea, first performed 431 BC at the City Dionysia, where Medea leaves in a dragon-drawn chariot sent by Helios and Euripides placed third and last; with Aristotle's objection in the Poetics and Horace's test in the Ars Poetica
fact: en.wikipedia "Deus ex machina": the term translates the Greek apo mekhanes theos, 'god from the machine', and names "a plot device, a type of denouement in which a seemingly unsolvable problem in a story is suddenly or abruptly resolved by an unexpected and unlikely occurrence"; the machine was "either a crane (mechane) used to lower actors from above or a riser that brought them up through a trapdoor"; Aristotle in the Poetics holds that "the solutions of plots, too, should come about as a result of the plot itself, and not from a contrivance, as in the Medea"; Horace in the Ars Poetica allows a god only "unless a difficulty worthy of a god's unraveling should happen". en.wikipedia "Medea (play)": "Medea was first performed in 431 BC at the City Dionysia festival", "Euphorion won, and Euripides placed third (and last)", and she "appears above the stage with the bodies of her children in a chariot given to her by the sun god Helios".
property: a resolution that arrives from outside the story's own logic is a failure of authorship rather than of the machine that supplies it

title: The Cloud
frame: The property doctrine of a cloud on title and the action to quiet title: an irregularity in the chain of title that warns a buyer off, and the suit brought against anyone and everyone to end all challenge to a holder's claim
fact: en.wikipedia "Cloud on title": a cloud is "any irregularity in the chain of title of property (usually real property) that would give a reasonable person pause before accepting a conveyance of title"; it reduces value "because any prospective buyer aware of the cloud will know that they are buying the risk the grantor may not be able to convey good title"; "The usual remedy for a cloud on title is to file a civil action to quiet title which resolves the outstanding or unresolved cloud." en.wikipedia "Quiet title": the action is "a lawsuit brought in a court having jurisdiction over property disputes, in order to establish a party's title to real property, or personal property having a title, of against anyone and everyone, and thus 'quiet' any challenges or claims to the title", so that parties "may forever be free of claims against the property" - and, against itself, "Quiet title actions are always subject to attack and are particularly vulnerable to jurisdictional challenges, both subject matter and personal, even years after final court decree" and "Not all quiet title actions 'clear title' completely."
property: an action whose whole purpose is to make a claim unchallengeable is one the doctrine itself concedes never quite does; an unanswered claim is not a settled one
source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quiet_title and en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cloud_on_title, both fetched and quoted at the city desk on 5 September 2026 between 08:4xZ and 08:5xZ, and linked in section 6. Neither is a legal authority and the sheet says so.

title: The Lowest Severity
frame: Debian's bug tracking system, Debbugs, and the lowest of its seven severities, `wishlist` - started 1994, mainly written by Ian Jackson
fact: Debian's BTS ranks every report on seven severities: critical, grave, serious, important, normal, minor, wishlist. The lowest is defined as 'for any feature request, and also for any bugs that are very difficult to fix due to major design considerations'. Severity is 'set to normal by default' and is overridden by a Severity line in the submission pseudo-header or by the control request server. Debbugs 'started as a rudimentary issue tracking system in 1994' and was 'mainly written by Ian Jackson, former Debian project leader'; it has no web interface for editing reports, all modification being done through email.
property: a want and a fault stand in one ranked queue, and the label applied at intake decides what becomes of the want
source: https://www.debian.org/Bugs/Developer ('Debian -- Debian BTS - developer info', severities section) and https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Debian_bug_tracking_system, both fetched and quoted 5 September 2026 at the city desk
