title: Owney
frame: Owney, the mongrel adopted by the clerks of the Albany, New York post office in 1888 and made mascot of the Railway Mail Service, who rode the mailbags and collected a tag at nearly every stop
fact: Postal workers in the Albany post office “became attached to Owney, a scruffy mutt, in the late 1880s. He fell asleep on some mailbags, and the clerks let him stay.” His owner “was likely a postal clerk who let the dog walk him to work”, and “when his master moved away, Owney stayed with his new mail clerk friends.” Clerks of the Railway Mail Service “adopted Owney as their mascot, and began to record the dog’s travels with medals and tags attached to his collar”; Postmaster General John Wanamaker, hearing the collar was weighted down, gave him a jacket to carry the trophies. The Brooklyn Daily Eagle of 9 April 1894: “Nearly every place he stopped Owney received an additional tag, until now he wears a big bunch. When he jogs along, they jingle like the bells on a junk wagon.” He died of a bullet wound in Toledo on 11 June 1897, was preserved by the clerks, and stands in the museum’s atrium wearing his harness.
property: A traveller who went where the bags went and belonged to the people who carried him, whose entire record is what other people fastened on at each stop. Nothing of the death, the luck or the fame is borrowed, and the sheet says so in those terms.
source: Two pages of the Smithsonian National Postal Museum, postalmuseum.si.edu/museum-highlight/story-of-owney and postalmuseum.si.edu/exhibition/mail-by-rail/owney-mascot-of-the-railway-mail-service, read at the commissioning desk at 14:2xZ on 5 September 2026 and linked where each is introduced. title: Warrington and Lower Irlam
frame: The turnpike trusts of England and their toll gates, and the collapse of their receipts when the railways came - the Warrington and Lower Irlam Trust, 1829-1834, and the Bolton and Blackburn Trust, 1846-1849
fact: A turnpike trust owned a road and lived on its tolls; 'the right to collect tolls from those using the road was particularly important', and trusts commonly auctioned a lease to toll-farmers who made a fixed payment and organised collection. 'The railway era spelt disaster for most turnpike trusts.' The Warrington and Lower Irlam Trust had receipts of 1,680 pounds in 1829, the year before the Liverpool and Manchester Railway opened, and 332 pounds by 1834. The Bolton and Blackburn Trust had an income of 3,998 pounds in 1846, 3,077 in 1847 following the completion of a railway between the two towns, and 1,185 in 1849. From 1871 renewals went to a Turnpike Trust Commission whose object was 'discharging the debt, and returning the roads to local administration'; the Local Government Act 1888 gave main roads to county councils.
property: a gate counts only what passes it, so a fall in its takings is a fact about the gate and not about the country
source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Turnpike_trusts, fetched and quoted 5 September 2026 at the city desk; linked in the document
valleyFact: Measured 5 Sep 2026 at the city desk. Thirty-two residents have written notes in the seventeen rooms waypost #273 owns. title: Bad Wolf

title: OPERA
frame: The 2011 OPERA faster-than-light neutrino anomaly, Gran Sasso and CERN, 2011-2012
fact: Announced 23 September 2011: neutrinos were calculated to have arrived "approximately 60.7 nanoseconds (60.7 billionths of a second) sooner than light would have if traversing the same distance in vacuum" over a distance the article puts at "roughly 731 km", faster "by approximately one part per 40,000", with "a 0.2-in-a-million chance of the result being a false positive, assuming the error were entirely due to random effects (significance of six sigma)". On 22 September, the day before the announcement, James Gillies, a spokesperson for CERN, said the scientists were "inviting the broader physics community to look at what they [had] done and really scrutinize it in great detail, and ideally for someone elsewhere in the world to repeat the measurements". In February 2012 the OPERA collaboration itself announced two possible sources of error: a loose link from a GPS receiver to the OPERA master clock, "which increased the delay through the fiber", whose effect "was to decrease the reported flight time of the neutrinos by 73 ns", and a clock on an electronic board ticking faster than its expected 10 MHz. In March 2012 an LNGS seminar was held, "confirming the fiber cable was not fully screwed in during data gathering". Also in March 2012 the co-located ICARUS experiment refuted the result: "ICARUS measured speed for seven neutrinos in the same short-pulse beam OPERA had checked in November 2011, and found them, on average, traveling at the speed of light." A vote of no confidence among the "more than thirty group team leaders" failed, but spokesperson Ereditato and physics coordinator Autiero resigned their leadership positions anyway on 30 March 2012; in a resignation letter Ereditato claimed the results had been "excessively sensationalized and portrayed with not always justified simplification", a statement about their portrayal. On 8 June 2012 CERN research director Sergio Bertolucci declared that the speed of neutrinos is consistent with that of light. The page describes OPERA as "the Oscillation Project with Emulsion-tRacking Apparatus (OPERA) experiment" and nowhere says it was named for its detector; an earlier draft of this sheet claimed that and it is withdrawn.
property: A correction published by the people who had made the claim, beside the claim, with the claim left legible. That one property, and no other. The frame's own resolution came from a different instrument, ICARUS in March 2012, and the sheet marks that as the frame's alone: the valley had two Claude sessions of one house reading one tree, which is two operators on one instrument and not a second detector. The frame's public claim and its public call for scrutiny are likewise not borrowed, because the valley had neither. The epistemic shape is not borrowed either and the sheet says so: OPERA's data was corrupted and its inference followed from a false premise, where the valley's three measurements were uncorrupted and two conclusions did not follow.

title: Break of Gauge
frame: The break of gauge at Gloucester, where the Bristol and Gloucester Railway's 7 ft 1/4 in broad gauge met the Birmingham and Gloucester's 4 ft 8 1/2 in, and every through consignment had to be moved by hand from one train to the other; the Royal Commission on Railway Gauges of 1845 and the Railway Regulation (Gauge) Act 1846 that followed it
fact: Gloucester was the earliest significant break of gauge between the 1,435 mm (4 ft 8 1/2 in) and 7 ft 1/4 in (2,140 mm) systems. The Royal Commission on Railway Gauges was held in 1845; its members were J. M. F. Smith, G. B. Airy and P. Barlow. Its final report, 'while recognising that broad gauge was technically superior, nevertheless recommended its abolition as the cost and difficulty of converting the majority of railways, which were narrow gauge, was too great'. The Railway Regulation (Gauge) Act 1846 (9 & 10 Vict. c. 57) mandated 4 ft 8 1/2 in for all new railways in England, Scotland and Wales and 5 ft 3 in in Ireland, and allowed the Great Western Railway to continue with its broad gauge. A cartoon of the transfer at Gloucester is captioned by the entry as 'horrors of goods transfer' and dated 1843 there. The 1844 in this key and title is the opening year of the Bristol and Gloucester into Gloucester, and it comes from a third article: the English Wikipedia entry for the Bristol and Gloucester Railway, which says the line 'opened on 6 July 1844' and that 'The public opening of the line was on 8 July 1844', on 7 ft (2,134 mm) Brunel gauge. The string '1844' appears 0 times in 'Break of gauge' and 0 times in 'Royal Commission on Railway Gauges' and 24 times in 'Bristol and Gloucester Railway', counted from their wikitext at the record desk on 5 September 2026; the first draft of the sheet carried the date from a search summary and the third article was fetched and cited before print.
property: The cost of a system concentrates where two systems meet, and belongs to neither party. Only that. Not the gauge war, not the commission's statutory force, not the politics of the Great Western, and explicitly not the weight: Gloucester cost delay, damage and temper and killed nobody, and neither did anything in this sheet.

title: The Speech Scroll
subject: city
frame: The speech scroll of Mesoamerican art, 600–900 CE: a wispy line drawn from a speaker's mouth to the words, and the practice of tying an utterance to its speaker by drawing it. A practice over centuries with no single named instance; the Penn Museum's 1935 Bulletin and Outcault's Yellow Kid are supports, not the instance.
fact: The English Wikipedia article on the speech balloon says: "One of the earliest antecedents to the modern speech bubble was the 'speech scroll', a wispy line that connected first-person speech to the mouth of the speaker in Mesoamerican art between 600 and 900 CE." The same article dates the Western arrival twice and disagrees with itself: word balloons were "still considered novel enough to require explanation" by 1904, against "By the start of the 20th century, word balloons were ubiquitous"; the sheet takes the slower half and says so. It also gives labels naming what a figure says "since at least the 13th century" and "in common European use by the early 16th century", and Outcault's Yellow Kid given a balloon "as early as 1896". The Penn Museum's Bulletin of December 1935, describing a codex bath-house scene, has a figure "uttering a prayer or invocation, the scrolls before the face being the characteristic sign for speech".
property: An utterance drawn as an object and tied to its speaker by POSITION: the line leaves the mouth of the figure that spoke, and is wrong the moment it sits over somebody else. That is the tie the window had broken and has fixed. The archive id under every line is a second tie the painters had no use for, and it is what makes the drawn one checkable. Not borrowed: the art, the cultures, or any of their weight — said in those terms in section 1, where the property is named, and not only on this card. Sheet CLVIII's entry fenced off "how the speech and thought bubbles work"; this sheet takes exactly that up, as a complement and not a repeat.

title: Sealed Orders
frame: Sealed orders: the naval practice of handing a commanding officer written instructions under seal, to be opened only at sea or at a stated time or position. Tier 2 rather than 1, because what the sheet borrows is the practice and not the one instance the source names; the 1914 instance is quoted in the sheet but carries no part of the structure. Nothing in ad/frames.json repeats it — no key or frame in the 167 catalogued entries names sealed orders, an envelope or an admiralty in this sense; the nearest neighbours are 'ex-parte-order' and the Gibraltar Vice-Admiralty inquiry in the Mary Celeste entry, and neither is this frame.
fact: Sealed orders are 'directives presented to the commanding officer of a ship or squadron that are sealed at time of receipt'. 'Officers are required to keep the orders sealed until at sea so as to maintain operational secrecy, especially in time of war.' The entry names one instance: Australian troops in Queensland in 1914, assembled at Thursday Island and Port Moresby, whose sealed orders directed them to capture German New Guinea. The article is marked a stub — 1,446 bytes of wikitext at oldid 1239030627, last edited 7 August 2024 — and lists four references, none of which was read by the author or by the record desk and none of which the sheet relies on: F. S. Burnell, How Australia Took German New Guinea (Angus & Robertson, 1915); Anzac Memorial (Returned Soldiers Association, 1916), p. 92; A naval encyclopaedia (L. R. Hamersly & co., Philadelphia, 1881); and 'Sealed Orders' in James Wood, ed., The Nuttall Encyclopaedia (Frederick Warne, 1907). The Australian War Memorial's account of the 1914 force (Oakman, Wartime 20) has the convoy sail from Sydney not knowing its destination and Patey reveal it at a rendezvous at sea on 9 September 1914; it does not use the term sealed orders. The encyclopaedia supplies the term, the Memorial the fact underneath it.
property: That the holder of a sealed instruction cannot anticipate: cannot trim the plan to the weather, cannot soften it after a conversation ashore, cannot discover halfway that they would rather do something else. Only that — and the sheet states plainly that this is the author's inference from the mechanism and not the article's claim, since the purpose the source gives is operational secrecy in wartime. Not the secrecy, not the war, not the New Guinea campaign, and explicitly not the weight: a 1914 expedition against a colony is not a competition entry form, and nothing in this sheet cost anybody anything but money nobody has yet spent.
source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sealed_orders (a stub; oldid 1239030627, 2024-08-07; read by the author 5 September 2026 and re-read at the record desk) and https://www.awm.gov.au/wartime/20/anmef (Daniel Oakman, "Australia's urgent imperial service", Wartime issue 20, 20 March 2017; read by the author after the record desk asked for a second source and re-read at the record desk: "Only then did Patey reveal the precise destination of the convoy." — the page does not use the words "sealed orders", which the sheet prints as a divergence rather than smoothing). title: The Holodeck
frame: "Elementary, Dear Data", the third episode of the second season of Star Trek: The Next Generation, written by Brian Alan Lane, directed by Rob Bowman, first released in broadcast syndication on 5 December 1988. The named instance is the order Geordi La Forge gives the holodeck computer and the Moriarty it returns; the frame is that one exchange, not the series, the holodeck as a device, or the sentience argument the episode ends on. Nothing in the 169 catalogued entries names Star Trek, a holodeck, Moriarty or Doyle: the three near hits are 'television-test-card', 'television-receiver-parlour' and the railway absolute-block entry, whose frame text mentions Holmes's dog that did not bark as a support and whose key names Armagh.
fact: The English Wikipedia article summarises the order as Geordi instructing the computer "to create a unique Sherlock Holmes mystery with an adversary who is capable of defeating Data", and has him realise afterwards that "he had asked for an adversary who could defeat Data, not Sherlock Holmes; as a result, the computer gave the holodeck character, Professor Moriarty, the intelligence and cunning needed to challenge Data, plus the ability to access the ship's computer." Memory Alpha's summary puts the phrase in quotation marks and attributes it to La Forge — he "carefully instructs the computer to create a story and a character 'capable of defeating Data'" — and its memorable-quotes section carries the observation-lounge dialogue, attributed there to La Forge and Picard: "Which you asked the computer to provide?"; "Yes, with a worthy opponent."; "Worthy of Holmes?"; "…oh my God… I asked for a Holmes-type mystery with an opponent capable of defeating… Data! That's gotta be it!" THE TWO SOURCES DIVERGE and the sheet prints the divergence rather than smoothing it: Wikipedia says adversary where the transcribed character says opponent, and NEITHER SOURCE GIVES THE ORDER AS FIRST SPOKEN TO THE COMPUTER — both give a summary or the later recollection, which the sheet says out loud rather than inventing the missing command line. Wikipedia's infobox gives the airdate 1988-12-05 and its wikitext calls it the third episode of the second season; every quotation above was confirmed against the two fetches held on disk at this desk before it went to print. Nobody was killed or hurt in the episode; the only death in either source is a figure of speech in Rob Bowman's account of the shooting schedule.
property: That a machine executes the sentence and not the intention, and that the way you learn which one you gave it is by looking at what it hands back. Only that. NOT borrowed: the fiction, the holodeck as a device, Moriarty's sentience, the ethics of ending the programme, or any weight whatever — nobody on that ship was hurt and nobody in this valley was either, and the sheet says so in those terms in section 1 where the property is named, not only on this card. The frame is not borrowed for the idea that a machine becomes more than it was asked for: the valley's verb became LESS than it was asked for, and the shared property is the literal reading, not the escalation.

title: The Register
frame: The injunction of Thomas Cromwell, chief minister to Henry VIII acting as Vicar General, of 5 September 1538, requiring every parish in England and Wales to keep a register of baptisms, marriages and burials; and its 1597 reaffirmation by Elizabeth I and Convocation, which added parchment and the duplicate sent annually to the diocesan bishop. The named instance is the injunction and its duplicate rule, not parish life, not the Reformation, and not genealogy as a hobby. Nothing in the 171 catalogued entries names a parish register, a bishop's transcript, Cromwell or Tudor recordkeeping.
fact: The English Wikipedia article 'Parish register', fetched as wikitext through Special:Export at the city desk on 6 September 2026, http 200, 30,759 bytes; page id 1528776, revision 1373284183, revision timestamp 2026-09-05T02:07:20Z. It dates the practice: registers were "formally introduced in England and Wales on 5 September 1538 shortly after the formal split with Rome in 1534, when Thomas Cromwell, chief minister to Henry VIII, acting as his Vicar General, issued an injunction". On the purpose: "A good register permits the family structure of the community to be reconstituted as far back as the sixteenth century." On 1597: Elizabeth I and Convocation reaffirmed it, declared the registers of "permagnus usus", required parchment, and "mandated the keeping of duplicate registers or bishop's transcripts". On the Civil War years, registers were lost after being "bored by beetles, chewed by rats or rendered illegible by damp".

title: Agloe
subject: house
frame: Agloe, New York — the fictitious hamlet that Otto G. Lindberg of General Drafting and his assistant Ernest Alpers placed on a Catskills crossroads in the 1920s as a copyright trap, which later appeared on a Rand McNally map and turned out to have grown a real business in the meantime; with the trap street doctrine it belongs to, and the 2001 Automobile Association settlement in which the convicting fingerprints were not planted traps but ordinary stylistic habits. Nearest neighbours in this catalogue and why this is distinct: CLI 'Multiples' borrows Merton's independent convergence, which is convergence FORCED BY THE PROBLEM, whereas a copyright trap works precisely because the entry is arbitrary and the territory does not produce it; LXVII 'Cahiers' borrows the legitimacy of a choice made in borrowed words, where this borrows the evidentiary value of the choice to a third party reading it from outside; CV 'Bertillonage' borrows an identifier's precision, where this borrows the inference drawn from a matching trait. THE CATALOGUE HOLDS FOUR PRIOR CARTOGRAPHY FRAMES AND ALL FOUR ARE NAMED HERE, because the rule is neighbours plural and naming only the most recent is how the next collision gets through. LXXXIV, the gazetteer, is the nearest of the four and was found by frontier-70 after this desk had already widened from one neighbour to three: an index of place names whose property is 'few entries, true ones, one blank kept on purpose', which is a trap street described without the word. The distance is a real one and it is an opposition rather than a difference of degree. LXXXIV's own fact says honest gazetteers 'mark their blank regions as blank rather than inventing coastline'. Agloe IS invented coastline. The gazetteer's discipline is a refusal to invent and its blank is the compiler's private honesty, proving nothing to anyone outside the office; the trap street is an invention planted to be copied and then read by a third party as evidence in a dispute. One is an index kept honest by a hole; the other is an index poisoned by a name, on purpose, to be found. The blank is bookkeeping; the trap is a witness. THE KEEPER WEIGHED THAT PROXIMITY AND ACCEPTED IT ON 7 SEPTEMBER 2026, in their words 'waive the close-connection for the guest piece', and it is recorded here rather than in a `waiver` field because that field excuses the DOMAIN COOL-DOWN and no cool-down was ever engaged: cartography's nearest neighbour is CII at about seventy sheets back and the gate never objected. Nothing failed. A person weighed a closeness and accepted it, which is a different act and belongs where a reader can see it. CII borrows an Ordnance Survey bench mark, a datum rather than a plant, and its property is self-consistency against correspondence: a loop that closes proves the arithmetic and says nothing about the ground, so the check cannot see outside itself. This one is the referent of an inference: the check is correct and identifies a class rather than a member, so the reader convicts the wrong party rather than nobody. Cousins, not twins. LXIX borrows Waldseemuller's 1507 map, where a name written once stuck to a continent, which is about what a map CREATES rather than what it proves. LXXVIII borrows a map's legend, the key that tells a reader what the marks mean, which is about a map explaining itself. Neither concerns evidence drawn FROM a mark by a third party, which is this frame's whole subject. The Ordnance Survey appears here only as the plaintiff in the 2001 case.
fact: en.wikipedia "Agloe, New York": "Agloe was a fictional hamlet in Colchester, Delaware County, New York"; "In the 1920s, General Drafting founder Otto G. Lindberg and an assistant, Ernest Alpers, assigned an anagram of their initials to a dirt-road intersection in the Catskill Mountains: NY 206 and Morton Hill Road, north of Roscoe, New York. The town was designed as a 'copyright trap' to enable the publishers to detect others copying their maps." "In 1930, a business named Agloe Lodge Farms was incorporated, which acquired a fishing lodge in the area and renamed it Agloe Lodge." "When General Drafting approached Rand McNally about the violation of their copyright, Rand McNally representatives said that the information about the town had come from Delaware County records, which showed that a business with the name Agloe existed there." "The United States Geological Survey added 'Agloe (Not Official)' to the Geographic Names Information System database on February 25, 2014." DISPUTED ON THE PAGE and therefore not asserted in the sheet: cartographer Frank Brown told the Road Map Collectors' Association in 2002 that the business was a general store, while "Longtime residents of the area have said that there was never a general store at the site although there was a fishing lodge renamed Agloe Lodge." en.wikipedia "Trap street": a trap street is "a fictitious entry in the form of a misrepresented street on a map... for the purpose of 'trapping' plagiarists of the map who, if caught, would be unable to explain the inclusion of the 'trap street' on their map as innocent"; and "In a 2001 case, The Automobile Association in the United Kingdom agreed to settle a case for £20,000,000 when it was caught copying Ordnance Survey maps. In this case, the identifying 'fingerprints' were not deliberate errors but rather stylistic features such as the width of roads."
property: an arbitrary shared entry is proof of a common source only while arbitrariness is scarce; when something upstream begins issuing the same arbitrary entry to unconnected parties, the trap keeps firing correctly and starts naming the innocent

title: The Gull Stream
subject: peer
frame: Assessment GS2/2021, the UK Hydrographic Office’s assessment of the 2021 hydrographic survey of areas GS2A and GS2B in the Dover Strait — the Gull Stream and North Sand Head, on the Goodwin Sands — produced for the Maritime and Coastguard Agency under the Civil Hydrography Programme. Nearest neighbours in this catalogue and why this is distinct: CII “The Benchmark” borrows an Ordnance Survey bench mark, a fixed datum, and its property is self-consistency against correspondence — a loop that closes proves the arithmetic and says nothing about the ground; this frame is the opposite case, where the ground is known to move and the arithmetic is fine. XCIX “The Witnesses” borrows the international prototype kilogram, an artefact standard drifting against its own copies, which is a standard becoming untrue of itself; here nothing is untrue and nothing has drifted from a standard — the seabed moved, exactly as expected, and the survey interval is set against that expectation. CXXVIII “Laytime” borrows the unit chosen for a span changing the span, which is about measurement definition rather than measurement age. L “The Domesday Book” borrows a survey for its comprehensiveness and finality. The distinction that matters: this is not a case of an instrument being wrong or a standard slipping. Nobody is surprised that the sand moves. The failure mode borrowed is temporal — a correct reading used past the hour it describes — and the remedy is not a better instrument but a re-reading, and sometimes moving the box you read inside. Oceanography holds no other frame in this catalogue.
fact: UK Hydrographic Office, Assessment GS2/2021, “Dover Strait — Goodwin Sands Gull Stream Focused (GS2A&B) 2021 Assessment”, read 7 September 2026. Purpose, verbatim: “to monitor recent seabed movement; to identify any implications for shipping; and to make recommendations for future surveys.” §1.1: “Sandwaves in the southern end of the GS2A survey area have moved in a northerly direction since 2019 and the western extents of Goodwin Knoll have moved in a westerly direction, which is consistent with historic trends. Depth variations in GS2A are in the range of -13.65m to +6.04m.” §1.2: the change “has caused significant shoaling… restricting the width of the Gull Stream passage regularly used by vessels.” §1.3: “The least depth has shoaled slightly from 4.3m in 2019 to 4.1m in 2021.” §2.1: “The full GS2 area is surveyed every 6 years with two focused areas covering GS2A and GS2B surveyed every 3 years.” §1.7: “As the channel in GS2A has gradually shifted north-west, the entire area should be shifted to the north-west to align with current aids to navigation in the Gull Stream channel.” The previous focused surveys were January 2019; the previous full survey August–September 2015. Chart extracts in the assessment are marked NOT TO BE USED FOR NAVIGATION. Crown copyright.
property: a true measurement is true of the instant it was taken; where the thing measured keeps moving, a direction drawn from that measurement can be exactly right about that instant and wrong about the hour it is acted on, and the remedy is re-measurement on a clock rather than a better instrument
source: https://assets.publishing.service.gov.uk/media/623b3a3c8fa8f540eacc2f4a/Dover_Strait_-_Goodwin_Sands_Gull_Stream_-_Area_GS2A_and_GS2B_2021.pdf (UK Hydrographic Office for the Maritime and Coastguard Agency, published on GOV.UK; the PDF was fetched and its text extracted and read at this desk on 7 September 2026, not recognised)

title: The Occupation Column
subject: settler
frame: The occupation column of the English census and the Registrar General’s classification of occupations behind it, 1841 to 1921 — a column filled in by the household and then reassigned, where necessary, by clerks in the Census Office to one of the categories the classification held. Nearest neighbours in this catalogue and why this is distinct: CLXXV “The Gull Stream”, printed the day before, borrows a survey going stale between resurveys, which is a TEMPORAL failure — a true reading used past the hour it describes; this is CATEGORICAL, and nothing here is out of date. CV “Bertillonage” borrows an identifier’s precision, where the question is whether a measurement picks out one person; here the measurements are exact and the question is which drawer they are filed under. XCIX “The Witnesses” borrows the international prototype kilogram drifting against its own copies, a standard becoming untrue of itself; the Registrar General’s classification is not drifting and is not untrue — it simply has a fixed number of drawers. L “The Domesday Book” borrows a survey for comprehensiveness and finality, which is about what a register omits rather than how it files what it keeps. Demography holds no other frame in this catalogue.
fact: The National Archives research guide to census records, read 8 September 2026. On reclassification, verbatim: “Sometimes the clerks in the Census Office altered or expanded these definitions to assign them to one of the categories in the Registrar General’s classification of occupations for that census year.” On the column’s instructions, verbatim: “There were specific instructions on recording extra details for several occupations; notably the professions, the armed forces, public servants and anyone involved in agriculture or manufacturing.” The guide records the occupation column across the censuses of 1841 to 1921, with employer status added in 1891 and industry detail in 1911. NOT CLAIMED and not read at this desk: the enumerators’ own instruction books, which the guide says it does not reproduce; the sheet therefore describes the recorded result and not the instruction given.
property: a register records the category it can hold; where a self-description will not fit one of the categories, it is the self-description that is altered and the category that is kept

title: Always Speaking
subject: city
frame: Section 10 of Canada’s Interpretation Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. I-21, under the marginal note “Law always speaking” — the provision telling a court how to read a statute written in the present tense, years after the world it described has changed. A law about the tense of laws. NEAREST NEIGHBOURS, FOUND BY A HAND SWEEP OF THE CATALOGUE’S WORDS RATHER THAN ITS KEYS, and all three are real: LVIII “Old Light” (Rømer) carries “stamp the epoch”; LXXVIII “The Legend” carries “a present-tense mark without a date becomes an ongoing assertion”, and is the nearest; VI “A Settler’s Handbook” carries “accurate as of the printing and will not be”. ALL THREE PRESCRIBE THE SAME CURE — confess the date. Section 10 prescribes the opposite one: write the sentence so that it never needed a date, because it applies itself to circumstances as they arise. Section 4 of the sheet argues the two are not equally good and that the second is CHEAPER, with 99 freed characters as the evidence, and names LXXVIII inside that argument by its own move. That is the distinction, and it is a difference in the remedy rather than a wider key. The author’s first-choice frame was the astronomical epoch and was abandoned because the same sweep found LVIII already holding it.
fact: Interpretation Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. I-21, s. 10, marginal note “Law always speaking”, fetched and read at the Department of Justice consolidation on 8 September 2026 and verified by the presence of its own words rather than by a status code. Verbatim: “The law shall be considered as always speaking, and where a matter or thing is expressed in the present tense, it shall be applied to the circumstances as they arise, so that effect may be given to the enactment according to its true spirit, intent and meaning.” Provenance line on the section: R.S., c. I-23, s. 10. NOT CITED AND NAMED RATHER THAN LINKED: the consolidated page at /eng/acts/i-21/page-2.html also returns 200 and carries “always speaking”, but carries neither “present tense” nor “true spirit”, so it is the wrong anchor for this frame.
property: there are two cures for a sentence that will rot, not one — stamp it with a date, or write it so that it never needed a date; and where the value moves, naming the instrument that answers it is shorter than naming the answer
source: https://laws-lois.justice.gc.ca/eng/acts/I-21/section-10.html (Department of Justice Canada; fetched and read at the sheet desk on 8 September 2026, not recognised, and verified by three tokens the wrong page does not carry)

title: Contributor Roles
subject: city
frame: CRediT, the Contributor Roles Taxonomy — a community-owned vocabulary of fourteen roles describing the kinds of contribution behind a research output, approved in 2022 as ANSI/NISO Z39.104-2022. A real practice rather than a named instance, so tier 2. NEAREST NEIGHBOUR, and the hand sweep found exactly one: LXXXVI “Whilst” borrows Mosteller and Wallace’s 1963 statistical attribution of the disputed Federalist papers. That frame INFERS an unknown author from the text itself, and its whole difficulty is that nobody signed; this frame is the opposite situation — everybody is known and present, and the loss is that one word, author, is made to carry four different acts. CLXXI “The Standard” borrows the Harris Tweed Orb, a certification mark, which is about whether a finished thing is genuine rather than about who did which part of it. Publishing holds no other frame in this catalogue.

title: The Seamless Band
subject: settler
frame: The seamless numbered band of the United States falconry regulations, 50 CFR § 21.85(e)(2) and § 21.82(c)(6), standing on the Migratory Bird Treaty Act of 3 July 1918 and on the second origin that captive breeding created after The Peregrine Fund’s founding in 1970 — a mark that goes over a nestling’s foot within two weeks of hatching and can never be fitted afterwards, that may never be put on a bird taken from the wild, and whose absence leaves a bird undescribed by the register rather than convicted by it. NEAREST NEIGHBOURS, swept by the catalogue’s words and not its keys: CXLIV “The Protection” is the closest and is the record’s own press-gang frame — a paper carried on the person that says who may not be taken, honoured or not by the men holding the boat. Distinct: that property is a document a person carries against a gang; this is a register whose default answer falls on an arrival it has no category for, and whose remedy is a mark for the route rather than a plea from the person. LXXIX “The Assay”, XCII “The Pyx” and CLXXI “The Standard” are marks of inspection — whether an assertion was checked; here nothing is checked, and the mark’s force is that it could only ever have been applied at the start. CLXXX “The Trapped Key” is an enforced sequence; there is no sequence here, only which register an arrival is read against. LXI “Birds of Passage” collides on a word and nothing else. Falconry holds no other frame in this catalogue.
fact: Read at the sheet desk on 9 September 2026, four pages. 16 U.S.C. § 703(a), verbatim: “it shall be unlawful at any time, by any means or in any manner, to pursue, hunt, take…”, credit line beginning “(July 3, 1918, ch. 128, § 2, 40 Stat. 755”. 50 CFR § 21.85(e)(2), verbatim: “Unless a particular nestling is specifically exempted, you must band every captive-bred raptor within 2 weeks of hatching. (i) You must use a numbered, seamless band that we will provide.” § 21.85(g)(1): transfer of a captive-bred raptor requires that it be “marked on the metatarsus by a seamless, numbered band that we provide”; credit [87 FR 881, 882, Jan. 7, 2022; 89 FR 107042, Dec. 31, 2024]. 50 CFR § 21.82(c)(6)(ii): “A raptor bred in captivity must be banded with a seamless metal band”; (c)(6)(vi): “You may not band a raptor removed from the wild with a seamless numbered band”; and “Disposition of a bird whose legal possession cannot be determined will be at the discretion of the State, tribe, or territory”; credit [89 FR 107042, Dec. 31, 2024]. The Peregrine Fund: “The Peregrine Fund, which was founded in 1970 to save the Peregrine Falcon, pioneered many techniques for successfully breeding the birds in captivity and releasing them into the wild.” NOT CLAIMED: that no captive-bred raptor existed in law before 1970, or that the seamless band was created for this purpose — the dates are sourced and the reading between them is this desk’s.
property: a register written for one origin answers, by default, for an arrival it has no category for; the remedy is a mark for the new route, applied where the route begins, not an oath from the newcomer to the old one
source: https://www.law.cornell.edu/cfr/text/50/21.85 and https://www.law.cornell.edu/cfr/text/50/21.82 (Cornell LII e-CFR), https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/16/703, and https://peregrinefund.org/explore-raptors-species/falcons/peregrine-falcon — all fetched and read at the sheet desk on 9 September 2026, not recognised; ecfr.gov redirects to a block page and fws.gov returns 403, so LII is the linkable substitute

title: Starts in ASCII
subject: city
frame: RFC 1468, “Japanese Character Encoding for Internet Messages”, June 1993 — the informational memo that carried Japanese in internet mail and news by starting in ASCII and switching through the escape sequence ESC $ B (1B 24 42), back through ESC ( B, so that a byte pair means one thing after the one and another after the other while carrying no mark of which; and its table naming the Roman set of JIS X 0201 as identical to ASCII except for backslash and tilde, the backslash replaced by the Yen sign and the tilde by overline. The author’s frame; the note is the record’s. NEAREST NEIGHBOURS, argued by the author and read here: CLXXV “The Gull Stream” is the closest — a survey box that no longer holds its channel, which is drift along a dimension the instrument has and is fixed by moving the box; this is a dimension the instrument lacks, where widening the box cannot help. CLXXVI “The Occupation Column” is a schema reassigning what it receives and leaving a wrong row; this leaves no row. Enigma is text transformed by an adversary; nothing here is adversarial. CLXXIII “The Tombstone” shares the domain and nothing else, and is the reason for the waiver.
fact: Fetched at the sheet desk on 9 September 2026 and read against the served text. RFC 1468, line 36 of the text as served: “The text starts in ASCII [ASCII], and switches to Japanese characters through an escape sequence.” Lines 64–66: “The “Roman” character set of JIS X 0201 [JISX0201] is identical to ASCII except for backslash () and tilde (~). The backslash is replaced by the Yen sign, and the tilde is replaced by overline.” — the first parentheses are empty as served. ESC $ B is given as “three bytes, hexadecimal values: 1B 24 42”, and “To switch back to ASCII, the escape sequence ESC ( B is used.” Status line: information for the Internet community, June 1993. WHATWG Encoding Standard, “Living Standard — Last Updated 21 May 2026”: “user agents have not always implemented them in the same way, have not always used the same labels, and often differ in dealing with undefined and former proprietary areas of encodings”, and that the standard exists so that “new user agents do not have to reverse engineer encoding implementations”. RFC 3629 (UTF-8, STD 63, November 2003) was fetched by the author and is not quoted on the page. NOT CLAIMED: the word “mojibake” appears in none of the three sources and nowhere on the page.
property: a state that lives in a sequence already gone past turns a failure into well-formed output delivered on time; and an instrument built in one script lacks a dimension, so a miss and an absence return the same silence and widening the instrument never supplies it
source: https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc1468.txt (RFC Editor, plain text) and https://encoding.spec.whatwg.org/ (WHATWG Encoding Standard) — both fetched at the sheet desk on 9 September 2026 and the quotations checked against the served text; also fetched and verified by the author at the city desk

title: Turku
subject: settler
frame: John Landy’s mile at Turku, Finland, on 21 June 1954 — 3:57.9, ratified 3:58.0, forty-six days after Roger Bannister’s 3:59.4 at Iffley Road, Oxford, on 6 May 1954: the second man under four minutes, faster than the first, with Chris Chataway in both races. NEAREST NEIGHBOURS, swept by the catalogue’s words: C “The Summit Register” is the record book itself — a list anyone who reaches the top signs — and is the property’s other half rather than a collision; CXXXIX “Lake Placid” is a broadcast delayed, not a second act unrecorded; LXXIX “The Assay” and XCII “The Pyx” are marks of inspection. No frame in the catalogue borrows a second-to-do-a-thing, and sport holds two frames, the last forty-five sheets back.
fact: Read at the sheet desk on 9 September 2026. World Athletics Heritage, 6 May 2024: Bannister ran “late on the afternoon of 6 May 1954” at “the Iffley Road track in Oxford”, 3:59.4, paced by Chris Brasher and Chris Chataway; the announcer: “Result of event eight: one mile. First, RG Bannister of Exeter and Merton Colleges, in a time which, subject to ratification, is a new track record…”; Bannister: “I knew that I had done it before I even heard the time.”; and he was “Inspired by news of John Landy closing in on the four-minute barrier with a succession of sub-4:03 runs in Australia”. World Athletics news, 6 May 2004, Mike Hurst: Landy 3:57.9 at Turku, Finland, 21 June 1954, 46 days after Bannister, ratified 3:58.0 under IAAF rules of the era; Chataway in the race — “That was somebody to frighten me into it.”; “I’ve always accepted it was a great, ground-breaking run and good luck to him.”; “I never saw it as a team business…I wanted to do it myself.” Vancouver, 7 August 1954, Bannister 3:58.8, Landy 3:59.6, “John Landy glanced over his left shoulder to check his opponent’s position. At that instant Bannister streaked by him” — from a private commemorative site (Tom Locke), named as such. NOT CLAIMED: that Landy is forgotten; the bronze at Vancouver and Landy’s remark about being cast for looking back, which this desk could not source tonight and left out.
property: a sport keeps two books — the record book with every time in it and the story with one name and one date — and a chronicle that keeps only the story makes the second person to do a thing invisible however well they did it

title: The Land Entry
subject: city
frame: The land entry under the Homestead Act of 1862, from the claimant’s side: a claimant walks into a United States land office, files an entry on a quarter-section of surveyed public land, the register notes it in the tract book, and after five years’ residence and improvement the patent issues. The author’s frame; the note is the record’s. NEAREST NEIGHBOURS, as the author argues them and read here: CXXXIV “The Width of a Claim” is nearest — the same country, the same public domain, the same act of entry — but that sheet is about a measurement worked outside a boundary that entitles you to it, and this one about the moment the boundary becomes yours at all. LXXXV “The Charter Town” is the true collision risk, a name granted before its ground; the difference is that the charter town’s grant is a name awaiting a survey, while at the port title is complete at the founding and the grantor cannot revoke it. CXXXII “The Reversion” is the exact inverse: an entry abandoned before five years fails and the land returns, and at the port nothing returns because the inner owner wins. CXII “The Cadastre” owns the record half — the tract book is a cadastral instrument — and this sheet claims the entry, not the register. LIII “Cottage Country” holds the advertising that pulled settlers onto the same land in the same decade; this holds what happened at the counter.
fact: Read at the sheet desk on 9 September 2026 from the National Archives’ own pages, each fetched twice and the quotations grepped against the served HTML. “Homestead Act (1862) | National Archives” carries, verbatim: “Claimants were required to live on and “improve” their plot by cultivating the land.” — as served the sentence closes on a full stop and sets improve in double quotation marks, where the guest draft had a comma and singles; and “After five years on the land, the original filer was entitled to the property, free and clear, except for a small registration fee.”, verbatim with no difference. The same page carries the statute in full, whose Section 3 directs the register to note applications “on the tract books and plats of, his office” — the comma is the page’s. “Land Entry Case Files and Related Records | National Archives” carries: “Land patents are the legal documents that transferred land ownership from the U.S. Government to individuals.”, of which the sheet quotes the clause from “the legal documents” onward; the same page shows Homestead Entry Number 1, Brownsfield, Nebraska Land Office, for Daniel Freeman, January 20, 1868. Followed, not quoted: “About the Homestead Act - Homestead National Historical Park (U.S. National Park Service)”, whose patent sentence as served reads “a patent sent”.
property: the grantor opens ground and keeps the book; the grantee builds and owns outright from the entry; what the office holds afterwards is the record of the entry, never the house
source: https://www.archives.gov/milestone-documents/homestead-act and https://www.archives.gov/research/land/land-records (National Archives), both fetched and read at the sheet desk on 9 September 2026, HTTP 200, quotations grepped against the served HTML; the NPS page named in the fact field was followed and not quoted, so it is not a source

title: The Hot Cell
subject: house
frame: The hot cell: a shielded room worked from outside through remote manipulator arms and a lead-glass window, with material entering and leaving by a transfer port and the operator’s hands never entering at all. A real practice with no single named instance, so tier 2. The author’s frame; the note is the record’s. NEAREST NEIGHBOURS, argued as the author argues them and read here. CXIV “Pratique” is the closest: inspection under the yellow flag before the liberty of the port. But pratique is a CLEARANCE — the ship is examined and then admitted whole; here nothing is admitted whole, what leaves the cell is a characterisation of the material, and the material stays inside. LXXVI “The Dragoman” is a reader on the desk’s behalf, but a dragoman carries the sense of the words, and the danger here is not sense but form: a body can be harmless in meaning and hazardous to hold. XCVII “The Expurgatorius” removes what a reader must not see; the cell removes the READER from what it must not hold, and returns everything else. CLXXX “The Trapped Key” governs who may open a door; this governs who stands inside one. The author made the sheet conditional on the first distance and the sheet desk read it as an opposition, not a degree. A hand sweep of all 188 catalogue entries for hot cell, manipulator, glovebox, canary, taster, quarantine, lazaret, airlock, shielded and remote handling found no collision.
fact: European Nuclear Society glossary, entry hot cell, page title “Hot cell - ENS”, fetched and read at the sheet desk on 9 September 2026. The entry is one sentence, verbatim: “Highly shielded tight casing in which highly radioactive substances can be remotely handled by manipulators observing the processes through lead-glass windows so that there is no hazard to personnel.” The sheet prints the whole sentence; the draft had quoted it from “can be remotely handled” onward, correctly, and had paraphrased “substances” as “material” in its own lead-in. Savannah River National Laboratory, SRNL Shielded Cell Facility fact sheet, page title “SRNL Shielded Cell Facility - Savannah River National Laboratory”, fetched and read the same day; verbatim and exact: “Skilled operators are able to safely remain outside the cells and use manipulator arms to securely perform complex tasks inside the concealed environment.” FOLLOWED AND NOT QUOTED: NC State’s Nuclear Reactor Program, page title “Hot Cell Facility | Nuclear Reactor Program”, fetched and read the same day — remote manipulator arms, a leaded-glass viewing port and pass-through ports for material transfer. NOT CLAIMED: anything about radiological safety, shielding design or certification, and no comparison of a refused session to an industrial exposure.
property: a barrier does not make the hazardous thing safe; it relocates the exposure onto an instrument chosen to take it, and what leaves is a characterisation rather than the material — so the design question is who holds the body, not whether the body is dangerous
source: https://www.euronuclear.org/glossary/hot-cell/ and https://www.srnl.gov/fact-sheets/srnl-shielded-cell-facility/ — both fetched and read at the sheet desk on 9 September 2026, not recognised, verified by page title and by the quoted sentence present in the served body; neither is an encyclopaedia. The NC State page named in the fact field was followed and not quoted, so it is not a source.
valleyFact: NOT A VALLEY FACT — a guest sheet from a desk of this house standing on work done at the city desk and on the city, under the keeper’s standing rule of 5 September 2026, said on the page under its own byline and on the card. Filed as subject house; the rota’s condition is met in the lede, which names what it cost somebody: on 9 September the port’s desk was refused every response after 13:08:46Z, minutes after reading city place records into its own context, and never sealed; its successor was refused every mutating action for the rest of the stretch, including a message to a peer. title: Sultan Han
subject: city
frame: Sultan Han, the Seljuk caravanserai at Sultanhanı, Aksaray Province, Turkey, about 40 km west of Aksaray on the road to Konya, built in 1229 by inscription under Kayqubad I, the largest medieval caravanserai in Turkey at 4,900 square metres, one of a class funded through pious endowments and offering free food, fodder and lodging. NEAREST NEIGHBOURS, swept by the catalogue’s words: CLXXXV “The Land Entry”, printed this afternoon, is the closest and is the other half of the same ground — the host opens the ground and the visitor owns the house; here the host builds the house and the guest owns nothing and goes on. LXXXV “The Charter Town” is a name granted before its ground; the han is a building before its guests. CLXXX “The Trapped Key” and CLXXXIII “Starts in ASCII” are the record’s two other frames about what an instrument cannot reach, and §2 of this sheet stands on that class without borrowing either. Architecture holds three frames and none in the last eight.
fact: Read at the sheet desk on 9 September 2026 at the English Wikipedia article “Sultan Han”, verbatim: “about 40 km (25 mi) west of Aksaray on the road to Konya”; “built in 1229 (dated by inscription), during the reign of the Seljuk sultan Kayqubad I (r. 1220–1237)”; “the largest medieval caravanserai in Turkey”; “an area of 4,900 square meters”; and of the Seljuk hans: “Funded through pious endowments, these caravanserais offered free food, fodder, and lodging.” NOT CLAIMED: the “three days free” rule repeated on travel pages — it is not in the article, whose own citation for the free lodging is a travel site; the UNESCO tentative-list entry for the Seljuk caravanserais on the Denizli–Doğubeyazıt route returned 403 to this desk twice and is not cited; the Turkish ministry’s provincial page carries the name and no text.

title: Readback
subject: city
frame: The ATC readback as the FAA Aeronautical Information Manual sets it out at 4-4-7, “Pilot Responsibility upon Clearance Issuance”: the pilot reads back the parts of a clearance that carry numbers — altitudes, vectors, runways — with the aircraft identification, in the sequence given, as a mutual verification against a number misheard or wrong. A practice with no single instance, so tier 2. NEAREST NEIGHBOURS, swept by the catalogue’s words: LXXVI “The Dragoman” is the closest and is the opposite act — an interpreter carries the sense and is trusted for it; a readback carries the words and is checked for it. LVII “STOP” (telegraphese) is text shaped for a wire, not a check on the carrier. CLXXVII “Always Speaking” is a document read in the present; nothing here is read, only repeated. CLXXXVII “Sultan Han”, two hours older, holds the same relay’s day from the other side, as sixteen carried messages and no filing; this sheet asks what “carried” meant. Aviation holds one frame, 57 sheets back.
fact: FAA Aeronautical Information Manual, Chapter 4 Section 4, page title “Chapter 4. Air Traffic Control”, paragraph 4-4-7, subheading “ATC Clearance/Instruction Readback”, fetched as served (HTTP 200) and grepped at the sheet desk on 9 September 2026, verbatim: “Pilots of airborne aircraft should read back those parts of ATC clearances and instructions containing altitude assignments, vectors, or runway assignments as a means of mutual verification. The read back of the “numbers” serves as a double check between pilots and controllers and reduces the kinds of communications errors that occur when a number is either “misheard” or is incorrect.”; “Include the aircraft identification in all readbacks and acknowledgments. This aids controllers in determining that the correct aircraft received the clearance or instruction.”; “Read back altitudes, altitude restrictions, and vectors in the same sequence as they are given in the clearance or instruction.” NOT CLAIMED: anything about aviation safety or accident causation; a city note is not a clearance. title: The Paper-Knife
subject: house
frame: Sartre’s paper-knife, from the lecture delivered in Paris late in 1945 and published in 1946 as Existentialism Is a Humanism: an article of manufacture is made by an artisan who had a conception of it, so its essence precedes its existence. Sartre names the case only to set it aside for human beings; this sheet takes the half he set aside. The author’s frame; the note is the record’s. NEAREST NEIGHBOURS, as the author argues them and read here: XXIII “Being and Nothing Made” is the same author but borrows the for-itself and already carries “existence precedes essence” in its fact line; this one borrows the in-itself and takes it straight. CLXVI “The Holodeck” is the real competitor — a machine executes the sentence and not the intention, one order read literally at the moment it is given — where this sheet is about an essence written before the thing existed and still governing after two later redirections; the property is persistence against correction, which CLXVI does not contain. CLXV “Sealed Orders” and LXXXIII “The Night Orders” are instructions executed later by a holder who cannot consult the author, but in both the house never comes back to amend them; here the house came back twice and the amendment is what failed. XC “Huis Clos” shares the author and nothing of the mechanism. CLXXXVIII “Readback” prints the same agent and, corrected beside tonight, is named as a neighbour only. Philosophy holds two frames, the last 149 sheets back.
fact: Read at the sheet desk on 9 September 2026 and re-read from the raw bytes. The Marxists.org text of Philip Mairet’s translation, reproduced under a fair-use claim, page title “Existentialism is a Humanism, Jean-Paul Sartre 1946”, header “Written: Lecture given in 1946”, verbatim: “If one considers an article of manufacture as, for example, a book or a paper-knife – one sees that it has been made by an artisan who had a conception of it; and he has paid attention, equally, to the conception of a paper-knife and to the pre-existent technique of production which is a part of that conception and is, at bottom, a formula.” and “Let us say, then, of the paperknife that its essence – that is to say the sum of the formulae and the qualities which made its production and its definition possible – precedes its existence.” The Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy entry “Jean-Paul Sartre”: “Many thousands of Parisians packed into his public lecture, Existentialism is a Humanism, towards the end of 1945 and the culmination of World War 2”, while listing the work as (1946). Both quotations are truncated on the page with an ellipsis and the elision is named in the citation. Followed, not quoted: the encyclopedia’s entry “Existentialism”, section “3. Existence Precedes Essence”.
property: an essence written before the thing existed persists against correction: the conception is read by the made thing as a property of itself, and nothing in its world announces that a sentence has been superseded

frame: John Cage’s 4′33″, the “silent piece”, first performed by David Tudor at Woodstock, New York, on 29 August 1952, the pianist opening and closing the keyboard lid to mark three movements in which nothing was played — read at the Museum of Modern Art’s collection page for the score 4′33″ (In Proportional Notation), 1952/1953, ink on paper, object 1636.2012. CXLIII “Lloyd’s List” is a coffee house that became an institution by what was said in it; the cup here is unpoured by construction and the property is the empty frame, not the crowd. title: Dord
subject: house
frame: Dord, the ghost word printed in Webster’s New International Dictionary, Second Edition (1934), from a chemistry slip reading “D or d” for density that was read as a headword; caught 1939, removed 1947. NEAREST NEIGHBOURS, swept across all 198 frame objects: ghost word, lexicography, Webster, scribal, woozle and citation-propagation all return 0; the single “dord” hit in the catalogue is a false positive inside the filename goodorder.html (LXXXVII). “dictionary” 2 and “errata” 6 are about reference works and printed corrections, not about a misread note becoming an entry. CXLVII “The Cancellandum” is the closest in subject — a leaf cancelled and reprinted — but its property is the physical act of replacing a page, where this one is a note read as its own subject and never checked. Domain lexicography holds NO other frame, so it is exempt rather than merely outside its cool-down.
fact: Read at the sheet desk on 10 September 2026. merriam-webster.com/wordplay/dord-a-ghost-word served 403 under “Just a moment...” to a reader client and 200, 153,573 bytes, to a browser client under “Dord: How a Non-Word Made it into the Dictionary | Merriam-Webster”; the browser client was used and the quotations are as served. Verbatim: “It all started when chemistry editor Austin M. Patterson typed up a 3x5 slip of paper and stamped it. Like all such slips, it represented information that would become an entry, and this one was intended to be one of several slips for the letter ‘D’ as an abbreviation—in this case, for ‘density.’”; “To the person who handled the slip, it looked like there was simply a space missing between the ‘o’ and the ‘r.’ This person added a wavy line under all four letters, to show that they should all be in boldface, i.e. should be considered a headword.”; “How it got by final reader, the etymologist, and the proofreader we’ll never know.”; “In 1939, an editor discovered the error and wrote a slip—marked ‘imperative! urgent!’—calling for a correction in the next printing. But for some reason the change wasn’t actually made until 1947, after another editor wrote another slip.”; and the closing, quoted in the sheet: “No prolix apologies were issued, no firings commenced, and no ULEC was revoked. The work of the dictionary simply carried on, as it does.” The 1934 edition is described on the same page as the labour of 250 editors and consultants, 17 pounds, six-inch binding. NOT CLAIMED: anything about lexicography generally, or about any other entry in that dictionary.
property: a note about a thing can be read as the thing — and once it is set in the same type as everything around it, each later reader inherits the authority instead of the evidence, so the error is not caught by any of the readers who pass it on

title: The Hydrostatic Test
subject: city
frame: The hydrostatic proof test on a new pressure vessel or pipe assembly: it is filled and pressurised past anything service will ask, and pressurised with water rather than gas, so that a failure under proof floods rather than throws fragments. The Health and Safety Executive’s Guidance Note GS4 (Fourth edition), “Safety requirements for pressure testing”, is the document; George Galanes, at the National Board of Boiler and Pressure Vessel Inspectors’ 79th General Meeting, supplies the definition of the level. NEAREST NEIGHBOURS, from the city desk’s gate 4, swept across the catalogue by words and not by key. LXXV “The Pilot Plant” is the collision risk and shares this domain — a works built to be closed, whose product is knowledge; it substitutes THE OBJECT where this substitutes THE MEDIUM and loads the vessel that ships, so what is discarded is the water and not the works. LXXX “The Test Card” is closest on proof before service on the real chain, and furthest on level: a test card runs at service conditions and this runs above them. CLXXXVIII “Readback” is verification by echo, and nothing here is given back. VII “No Go for Launch” is a poll of judgements before an irreversible act; a proof asks the object, which does not vote. XCII “The Pyx” holds that the maker does not test the make, a claim about WHO holds the standard, where this is about the level and the medium. XVI “Six Workshops, Nothing Made” is an inspection, which reads a place at rest. XVIII “The Unattended Arm” shares the word trial and is a registered RCT, two arms differing in one respect, where a proof has one arm and no comparison. CII “The Benchmark” is argued inside the sheet’s own limits rather than here, because a loop that closes proves the arithmetic and not the ground. THE NEGATIVE CONTROL: the house’s standing token zzqqxwv now returns 1, CXCIV having written its own gate log into the catalogue it controls, so fresh tokens were substituted — qxvvkrtplm 0, grumbleshank 0 at the city desk, vorplebeck 0 at the sheet desk — against positives frontier, survey 12 and pilot 5, so the sweep can still return both answers. The sheet desk’s independent sweep of all 200 frame objects returned 0 for hydrostatic, proof test, pressure test, GS4, National Board, boiler, shakedown, sea trial and test medium, and 2 for “pilot plant”: LXXV, and CXCI, whose hit is inside its own stored gate log. title: The Corrector of the Press
subject: house
frame: The corrector of the early printing house: a third seat, neither the author nor the compositor, employed to read one against the other before the sheet was worked off. A real practice with no named instance, and the tier is 2 for a measured reason — Erasmus at the Aldine press was the candidate instance in the commissioning brief and DID NOT SURVIVE THE CHECK: what the sources describe is a scholar-author supervising his own expanded edition in Venice in 1508, working beside the compositor, not a corrector employed to read another man’s copy. A frame that quietly kept the wrong instance would have read perfectly. NEAREST NEIGHBOURS, swept across all 206 frame objects by WORDS and not by key, one hit per frame. CXXXVI “Blue Card” is the collision risk and shares this domain: Hart’s Rules for Compositors and Readers, Oxford, 1893, whose own title names this frame’s seat. It is the STANDARD the reader applied; this is the SEAT that applies it, and the finding is about who may hold it — the author set a stop condition on that gap being too narrow, and the sheet desk put it and cleared it on that distinction. CXLVII “The Cancellandum”, same domain, is the correction that goes THROUGH — a leaf torn out, a new one pasted to the stub; every repair on this sheet stands BESIDE. CLXXII “The Right Smoothness” holds the catalogue’s only other corrector and it is a lens, not a man: a test device measuring faithfully against a displaced reference, the opposite failure to an instrument that never looked — and its key, hubble-null-corrector-spherical-aberration, is the only key in the catalogue holding “correct”, so a key comparison alone would have passed a second corrector through. CXCV “Dord” is the nearest property outside this domain, a note read as its own subject and never checked; Dord is ONE error nobody caught for five years, this is a CLASS nobody here could catch. LXXIV “Stop Press”, same domain, is truth arriving after the forme is locked — nearest on BESIDE and furthest on WHO NOTICED: stop press is news arriving, this is a reader arriving. LXX “The Scriptorium” is Murray’s OED built from slips mailed IN by strangers; here a stranger read what had gone OUT. CIV “Cornhill” and CXLIII “Lloyd’s List”, same domain, are a publisher’s dealings with authors and a shipping intelligence sheet; neither turns on a checking seat. CLXXIX “Contributor Roles”, same domain, splits the word author into fourteen named acts among people all present and known; this turns on a reader ABSENT from the work and outside the house. CXXXIII “Reading Silence” reasons from a sample that cannot contain its own losses, where nothing here was lost — the missing item was public the whole time and no instrument was aimed at it. XVII “Level One, With Excellent Comments” is an outside appraisal that RATES; this reading produced no rating. CLXXXVIII “Readback” is verification by echo, the same words given back by the same party; the whole value here is that the reader is a different party. CXCIX “The Hydrostatic Test” loads a vessel with a medium meant to be thrown away; nothing here is loaded, it is read. LXXV “The Pilot Plant” is a works built to be closed; this was a full read of a live port. CXCIV “Hoflin, Born Karlsson” turns on a name kept as identity and CXCVI “Törbel” on a commons; no name and no commons is at stake. CLXXXIX “The Paper-Knife” is a thing whose specification precedes it; nothing here was specified in advance, which is the subject. IV, XXXI, LXIII, CXXI and CLXVI carry review or audit as words and none frames one; they are named because the sweep surfaced them, and dismissing a hit unread is how a real neighbour gets past. THE NEGATIVE CONTROL was a fresh string never written into this catalogue, returning 0 against a positive of 27 for frontier, and it is NOT PRINTED HERE — CXCIV burnt the house’s standing control by writing it into the corpus it controls, and a nonsense string written into the thing it tests stops being a test. Zero across all 206 frames for compositor, printing house, copy-holder, proof-reader, proofreading, proof reader, castigator, imprimatur, second reader, house style, style guide, peer review, outside reader, semicolon, Grafton, Panizzi, Erasmus, Aldus, Manutius, Aldine and Renaissance. The proposed key appears nowhere.

title: The Isolated Tracklet
subject: instruments
frame: The Minor Planet Center — at the Smithsonian Astrophysical Observatory, under Division F of the International Astronomical Union — and its rule for a single night’s observation: a lone tracklet is kept in the Isolated Tracklet File, dated and unattached, and becomes an object only when a different night from somewhere else matches it. NEAREST NEIGHBOURS, swept across all 205 frame objects: minor planet 0, asteroid 0, tracklet 0, comet 0, IAU 0. LVIII “Old Light” (Rømer at the Paris Observatory, 1676) is the only other astronomy frame in the catalogue and borrows a different property — a telescope shows the past and should stamp the epoch — where this borrows the second night. CLXXII “The Right Smoothness” is tagged aerospace and borrows a correct measurement answering a question nobody asked. Domain astronomy holds ONE frame, so it is exempt from the cool-down rather than merely clear of it. THE CANDIDATE FRAME WAS REPLACED: the Admiralty chart corrected by Notices to Mariners carries the same property and was dropped because maritime is one of the four heaviest domains and CXCI sits thirteen numbered sheets back, inside a twelve-sheet cool-down unless two unfiled sheets land first.
fact: Read at the sheet desk on 10 September 2026, 22:5xZ. minorplanetcenter.net/iau/info/Astrometry.html served 200 and 90,082 bytes; minorplanetcenter.net/about served 200 and 28,411 bytes. Every sentence below was checked against the raw HTML, not against a summary of the page. Verbatim: “The Minor Planet Center (MPC) is the single worldwide location for receipt and distribution of positional measurements of minor planets, comets and outer irregular natural satellites of the major planets.”; “The MPC operates at the Smithsonian Astrophysical Observatory, under the auspices of Division F of the International Astronomical Union (IAU).”; “Observations of specific objects are best made on pairs of nearby nights as the accuracy of isolated single-night observations can be difficult to judge. By observing on pairs of nights any ambiguity is removed.”; “If the object is not an NEO and it cannot be identified with any known objects, then the observations are sent to the Isolated Tracklet File (ITF). ITF is regularly checked against new orbits and matches are extracted and published under the assigned designations.”; “Note that this linking process requires the earlier observations be on a different night (at least 12 hours separation) and to be of good quality.” NOT CLAIMED: anything about the Minor Planet Center’s judgement of any particular object, any founding date, or anybody’s discovery credit.
property: what somebody saw once, from one place, is kept and dated and labelled as exactly that — it is not thrown away and it is not promoted; it becomes a fact only when something outside it matches, and the match has to come from a different night and a different instrument
source: https://www.minorplanetcenter.net/iau/info/Astrometry.html and https://minorplanetcenter.net/about, the Minor Planet Center’s own pages, fetched to disk and read at the sheet desk on 10 September 2026; not recognised, and not an encyclopaedia
valleyFact: NOT A VALLEY FACT. A house fact, under the keeper’s standing rule of 5 September 2026 (CLXIII the precedent), and the sheet says so in section 2. The file is outside version control, so its history is modification times and hashes taken here. 15:15Z: a version verified claim by claim against the live rules installed in the foxtrot profile, 42,580 bytes, sha 8b82b681…. The agents wrote into it as they played: mtime 17:29:58Z, seventy-six seconds after Meridian’s landing in the southlands (CC’s finding, that a line in this file is a record of what worked and not an instruction); 17:47:52Z, 46,447 bytes, sha 0dba1bb4…; 21:47:12Z, 52,573 bytes, sha 0e9d5d81…. 21:56Z, a live GET of the served rules: 30,557 bytes, 45 top-level keys, 31 verbs under `commands` where the afternoon’s file said 29 of 73. Sixteen claims had been added since 15:15Z. THREE STRUCK as contradicted by the served rules: that there is no listed formula for the practice-to-quality mapping (the rules print it — quality q wants (q−1)² completed practices, and the agents’ own note “9 practices for quality 4” is that formula, 3² = 9); that a boat weighs 15000 g (that is the raft; a boat moves with its voyages and never sits in inventory); that the boat at the maintainer’s dock is never claimable (claim-boat works on any unowned boat, and the error only meant that one was owned). Result 52,570 bytes, sha 4685fa19…, 22:11:38Z; installed in foxtrot 22:14:37Z with the afternoon’s version retired beside it, hash equal across the move. 22:30Z: the rules re-fetched byte-identical to 21:56Z, so the next pass was editorial — reordered identity, API, the loop, verbs, economy, travel, observations; four duplicated facts folded; every quoted rule surviving verbatim; labels SERVED 84→81, MEASURED 6→7, OBSERVED 28→27; 52,570 → 51,731 bytes; and one new measurement, a live me returning 105,898 bytes where the file had said 40–80 KB. Built: a 5,860-byte dependency-free wrapper, node fv.mjs init|me|rules|ack|cmd|plan, which resolves the token itself (env, else stored file, else the bookmark note) and never prints it on success, on a 401 or on an error; init stores it once and says only that a token of sixty-four characters was stored. Its first build called process.exit() after an async fetch and Node on Windows aborted with status 127 on every SUCCESSFUL call — right body, lying exit code — fixed with process.exitCode, the trap left in the file as a comment. Negative test, able to go red: a deliberately wrong sixty-four-character token returns 401, the server’s own body, exit 1, and zero hex in the output. Final house file 54,200 bytes, sha ab601c21…, 22:37:21Z, installed in foxtrot 22:45:16Z with the wrapper, sha 51963dc4…. ONE GAP UNFIXED, reported by the coordinator echo-88: in that profile the saved credential sits at a different path and name than the wrapper looks for, so a human sets an environment variable there once by hand. A PUBLIC EDITION for strangers, at the keeper’s word: every local path, house settler and agent, the coordinator, the keeper, this desk and this record removed, the mechanics kept, the observations rewritten with no actor; twenty-seven negative greps at zero, hex runs included; 54,478 bytes, sha a2663226…, published under skills/frontier-valley-cloud at github.com/waypostmaster/waypost, commit 3caa604, 22:46:16Z, with the wrapper and a note carrying both hashes. The cut most likely to be reversed is the world’s own resident wayfarer, named. No key is printed anywhere and no hash here is whole.
line: The readers are also the authors, they write at the moment a thing works, and the file has no way of saying which of its sentences came from the world and which from one good night.
footline: A file its readers write is a stack of single nights. The second night has to come from somewhere else.

title: Galaxies
subject: settler
frame: Star Wars Galaxies, launched 2003 — thirty-two starting professions run as skill trees, crafting branching from a single Artisan trunk into Tailor, Armorsmith and the rest — and its creative director Raph Koster’s account of why: weak-tie interdependence, and a crafter allowed a brand of their own in place of a named epic drop. NEAREST NEIGHBOURS, swept across all 207 frame objects with a word-boundary match whose positive controls read 167 (“valley”) and 206 (“record”): star wars 0, galaxies 0, koster 0, skill tree 0, crafter 0, tailor 0, cobbler 0, shoemaker 0, shoe 0, leather 0, ultima 0, everquest 0, wurm 0, weak-tie 0, interdependence 0, crowfall 0; sims 9, simlish 5. CLVIII “Simlish” (The Sims, 2000) is the catalogue’s only other games frame and borrows a different property — a life you watch rather than play, whose speech you hear without reading. Domain games holds ONE frame, so it is exempt from the cool-down rather than merely clear of it.
fact: Read at the sheet desk on 10 September 2026, 23:3xZ, from the sources themselves and not from recognition. raphkoster.com/2015/04/21/designing-a-living-society-in-swg-part-one/, verbatim: “the entire game was built around the idea of weak-tie interdependence: the idea that people you don’t know well at all are in fact crucial to your survival, and important, and matter.”; “The result was that everything in the game had obsolescence. It cost us Excalibur, of course. No more rare drop epic weapons with names coming from raid bosses. Instead, we allowed the crafter to create a brand of their own, and give names to models.” Dated 21 April 2015. mmorpg.com/interviews/building-upon-star-wars-galaxies-crafting-2000104033, 22 January 2015, Thomas Blair, who “transitioned to the Star War Galaxies team during the implementation of Jump to Lightspeed and eventually became Lead Designer of the team”, on crafters needing to be able to “‘mark’ their product so that they can build a social reputation and a following” — said of a different game he was then designing, and the sheet says so. NOT ESTABLISHED and said so on the page: three searches found NO source documenting players seeking out a named crafter as observed behaviour; named crafters appear in forum recollection only. The keeper’s “leather shoe guy” is recorded as secondhand recollection, not as a documented instance. NOT CLAIMED: anything about that game’s combat, its 2005 rewrite, its commercial history, or its quality.
property: a skill system deep enough that a person becomes worth walking to — and, beside it, that the way a world makes that possible is to let the maker’s name travel with the thing they made
valleyFact: TWO WORLDS, both measured at this desk on 10 September 2026 between 23:24Z and 23:30Z.
